# Netdryrun: full documentation

> Netdryrun is an open-source tool that tests network changes in a real virtual lab before they reach production. It boots the topology with containerlab, waits for convergence, checks BGP sessions, prefixes, routes and reachability, and returns a pass/fail verdict with evidence. It runs locally, in GitHub Actions, or as an MCP server for AI agents.

Install: `pip install netdryrun` · Source: https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun · Docs: https://netdryrun.com/



---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/

# Fail CI on routing mistakes before they reach production

To test a network change in CI, keep the changed configs and a containerlab topology in Git, describe the expected behavior in a `netdryrun.yml` file, and run `netdryrun run` (or the GitHub Action) on every pull request. Netdryrun™ deploys the lab, waits for BGP to converge, checks sessions, prefix counts, routes and pings, then destroys the lab. Any failed check exits non-zero and fails the job, with a JSON evidence file showing every command and its raw output.

[Try it in your browser](https://codespaces.new/netdryrun/netdryrun?quickstart=1){ .md-button .md-button--primary } [View the source on GitHub](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun){ .md-button }

The browser trial runs in GitHub Codespaces: it needs a free GitHub account, takes a few minutes to start, and then `bash examples/agent-demo/demo.sh` shows a bad change rejected and the fix accepted. Nothing to install.

!!! abstract "What Netdryrun is"
    Software teams don't ship code without running its tests. Network changes deserve the same step: run the change in a real lab, check how the network behaves, and ship only on a pass. Netdryrun is the open-source tool that makes that one command, one CI step, or one tool call for an AI agent. It tests network changes in a real virtual lab before they reach production. It boots the topology with containerlab, waits for convergence, checks BGP sessions, prefixes, routes and reachability, and returns a pass/fail verdict with evidence. It runs locally, in GitHub Actions, or as an MCP server for AI agents.

## A failing run

This is the bundled `frr-bgp-broken` example. Router r2 has a bad change: it sends r1 a default route.


```text
$ netdryrun run examples/frr-bgp-broken
Deploying lab ndr-frr-broken (3 nodes)...
  [PASS] r1: BGP session to 10.0.12.2 is established -- state is established (6.3s)
  [PASS] r1: ping 192.168.3.1 from 192.168.1.1 expects success -- 3/3 replies (2.3s)
  ... (3 more passing checks trimmed)
  [FAIL] r1: route 0.0.0.0/0 via bgp is absent -- unexpectedly present via bgp (not selected) (0.1s)
FAILED: 5 passed, 1 failed (6 checks)
```

The leaked default route was *received but not selected*: r1 kept its own default, so traffic still flowed and the ping passed. A ping test or a session check would have missed it. (A static analyzer such as Batfish also catches this particular leak; the [Batfish page](batfish.md) shows one that it misses and the lab catches.) Netdryrun counts a route that is in the routing table but not selected as present, so the "must be absent" check fails.

The check that caught it:

```yaml
- type: route        # nothing should send r1 a default route
  node: r1
  prefix: 0.0.0.0/0
  protocol: bgp
  present: false
```

Checks like this one run only after the network has converged (the positive checks passed and every configured BGP session on the node is up) and must hold for a time window, so they cannot pass just because BGP has not come up yet. See [convergence semantics](reference/config.md#convergence-semantics).

## Run it in GitHub Actions

```yaml title=".github/workflows/network-dryrun.yml"
name: Network dry run
on: pull_request
jobs:
  dryrun:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: netdryrun/netdryrun@v0.3.1
        with:
          path: network/        # folder containing netdryrun.yml
```

The action installs containerlab, runs the checks, writes a summary to the job page, uploads the JSON and JUnit reports as an artifact, and fails the job if any check fails. Details: [GitHub Action](github-action.md).

## Run it locally

Fastest start on your own topology: `netdryrun record my-lab/topology.clab.yml --deploy` snapshots today's behavior into checks, then `netdryrun run my-lab` tests every change against it.


```bash
pipx install netdryrun          # Ubuntu 24.04+: sudo apt install pipx && pipx ensurepath first
netdryrun run path/to/folder    # the folder containing netdryrun.yml
```

Requirements: Linux or WSL2, Docker, containerlab, Python 3.10+. Walkthrough: [Getting started](getting-started.md).

!!! warning "What a lab cannot prove"
    A pass means the change behaved correctly in a lab built from container router images (FRR, Nokia SR Linux, SONiC, Arista cEOS). That is strong evidence for protocol logic and policy intent. It is not proof of:

    - vendor-specific behavior on the routers you run in production
    - behavior at production scale (full tables, many peers)
    - hardware and ASIC limits
    - timing and convergence at scale

    More on this in [Trust and security](trust.md#what-a-lab-cannot-prove).

## Status


Version 0.3.1. Works with FRR, Nokia SR Linux, SONiC and Arista EOS (bring your own cEOS image) on Linux and WSL2. Check types: `bgp_session`, `bgp_prefixes`, `route`, `bgp_route` and `ping` (IPv4/IPv6 unicast BGP sessions, prefix counts, routes, BGP best-path attributes and ping), plus link-down, node-isolation and route-injection (FRR only) failure scenarios. On the [verdict corpus](corpus.md) v1 (30 realistic BGP changes: 19 harmful, 11 safe), Netdryrun judged 24/30 correctly, ping-only checks 20/30 and all-sessions-up checks 15/30. Netdryrun approved 5 of the 19 harmful changes (ping-only checks: 10 of 19) and blocked 1 of the 11 safe ones. On v2 (18 cases written after v1 to target v1's misses): Netdryrun 17/18, ping-only 9/18, all-sessions-up 7/18. Expected verdicts were committed before any run, on one FRR topology; method, every miss and a one-command rerun are on the corpus page. Provenance: both ran on Netdryrun 0.3.1. Issues and feedback: [github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/issues).


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/getting-started/

# Getting started

## Try it in your browser

No install: [open Netdryrun in GitHub Codespaces](https://codespaces.new/netdryrun/netdryrun?quickstart=1) and click **Create codespace**.

GitHub starts a Linux machine with Docker, containerlab 0.81.1 and Netdryrun installed from the repository, and pulls the FRR image the examples use. This takes a few minutes the first time. When the creation log shows `Ready`, run this in the terminal:

```bash
bash examples/agent-demo/demo.sh
```

The [agent demo](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples/agent-demo) boots four FRR routers twice, which takes about 65 s. The first change opens the filters to make a ticket work and is rejected by the leak guards; the second adds two prefix-list lines and passes all 14 checks. The run ends with `Demo OK`. The other FRR examples (`netdryrun run examples/frr-bgp`, `examples/frr-bgp-broken`) work the same way.

The codespace runs on the 2-core machine and uses your GitHub account's free Codespaces allowance (GitHub Free includes 120 core-hours and 15 GB of storage a month, so about 60 hours on this machine; Pro includes 180 core-hours). Stop or delete the codespace when you're done ([github.com/codespaces](https://github.com/codespaces)) so it doesn't use more. VM-based nodes (vrnetlab) don't work in Codespaces, which has no nested virtualization.

## Requirements

| Requirement | Notes |
|---|---|
| Linux or WSL2 | containerlab runs on Linux. On Windows, use WSL2. |
| Docker | The lab nodes are containers. |
| [containerlab](https://containerlab.dev/install/) | Netdryrun™ drives the `containerlab` CLI; it must be on `PATH`. |
| Python 3.10+ | |

containerlab needs root (or a user in the right groups) to create the lab. Run Netdryrun the same way you run containerlab on that machine.

!!! note "WSL2 and /mnt/c"
    If your topology lives under `/mnt/...` (a Windows drive), Netdryrun keeps containerlab's lab directory on the Linux filesystem (`~/.cache/netdryrun/labs`) unless you set `CLAB_LABDIR_BASE` yourself. SR Linux cannot save its config on a Windows drive.

## Install

```bash
pipx install netdryrun
netdryrun --version
```

On Ubuntu 24.04 and Debian 12 a plain `pip install` outside a virtualenv is refused ("externally managed environment"), so use pipx: `sudo apt install pipx && pipx ensurepath`, then open a new terminal. `uv tool install netdryrun`, or `pip install netdryrun` inside an activated virtualenv, work too.

The MCP server for AI agents is included: run `netdryrun mcp`. See [AI agents](ai-agents.md).

## Run the examples

The repository ships these example labs. The FRR and SR Linux images are pulled automatically on first use.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun && cd netdryrun
netdryrun run examples/frr-bgp          # 3 FRR routers, should pass
netdryrun run examples/srl-frr          # SR Linux + FRR, should pass
netdryrun run examples/frr-bgp-broken   # a bad change, should fail
examples/agent-demo/demo.sh             # replay: a leaky change rejected, the fix accepted
```

`examples/sonic-frr` needs the `docker-sonic-vs` image, which is on no container registry: download it from the SONiC build server and `docker load` it first ([how](guides/sonic-ci.md#1-get-the-image)). Then:

```bash
netdryrun run examples/sonic-frr        # SONiC + FRR, should pass
```

`examples/arista-frr` needs a cEOS image you download from Arista and import yourself; see the [examples page](examples.md#arista-frr).

Each run deploys the lab, runs the checks, prints one line per check and destroys the lab. The first run of an example takes longer while its images are pulled.

### Expected results

The [examples page](examples.md) has every example, what it shows and how long it takes.


| Example | Topology | Checks | Expected | Exit code |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `examples/frr-bgp` | Triangle of three FRR routers (r1, r2, r3), eBGP | 2 sessions, prefix count 1 to 10, route present via BGP, ping, best-path AS path and next hop, default route absent, and a link-failure scenario (reroute via r3) | `PASSED: 11 passed, 0 failed` | `0` |
| `examples/srl-frr` | Nokia SR Linux (`srl1`) peering eBGP with FRR (`frr1`) | 2 sessions, a BGP route on each side, a ping in each direction, best-path attributes on `srl1` | `PASSED: 7 passed, 0 failed` | `0` |
| `examples/sonic-frr` | SONiC VS (`sonic1`, configured by `setup` commands) peering eBGP with FRR (`frr1`) | a session, a BGP route on each side, a ping, a prefix count, best-path attributes, a port-down scenario | `PASSED` | `0` |
| `examples/frr-bgp-broken` | Same triangle, but r2 adds `default-originate` toward r1 | The first 6 checks of `frr-bgp`, without the scenario | `FAILED: 5 passed, 1 failed`; the default route check fails | `1` |

The broken example is the one shown on the [home page](index.md#a-failing-run). r1 receives the leaked default route but does not select it, so the ping still works. The route check catches it because a received-but-not-selected route counts as present.

SR Linux takes longer to boot, so `examples/srl-frr` sets `timeout: 120`.

## Record a baseline of your own lab (fastest start)

Point `record` at any containerlab topology you already have:

```bash
netdryrun record my-lab/topology.clab.yml --deploy
```

It deploys the lab, waits for BGP to converge, and writes `my-lab/netdryrun.yml` with a check for every established BGP session, every prefix count and every BGP route (up to 50 per node). Then make your change and run:

```bash
netdryrun run my-lab
```

Anything that changed fails, with evidence. Before committing the baseline, remove what is allowed to change and add negative checks for what must never happen (for example `present: false` for a default route at a peer). See the [`record` reference](reference/cli.md#record) and the [tutorial](tutorial.md).

## Write checks for your own lab

Put a `netdryrun.yml` next to your containerlab topology:

```yaml title="netdryrun.yml"
lab: topology.clab.yml      # your containerlab topology
timeout: 90                 # seconds a positive check may wait for convergence

checks:
  - type: bgp_session
    node: r1
    neighbor: 10.0.12.2
  - type: route
    node: r1
    prefix: 192.168.3.0/24
    protocol: bgp
  - type: ping
    node: r1
    source: 192.168.1.1
    target: 192.168.3.1
```

Check the file without starting anything, then run it:

```bash
netdryrun validate .
netdryrun run .
```

To debug a failing run, keep the lab up with `--keep` (or `--keep-on-failure`), inspect the routers, and rerun the checks against the running lab with `netdryrun check .`. Destroy it afterwards with `containerlab destroy -t topology.clab.yml --cleanup`.

Next: the [tutorial](tutorial.md) walks through all of this on a real lab, step by step. Then see the [netdryrun.yml reference](reference/config.md), the [CLI reference](reference/cli.md) and [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md).


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/tutorial/

# Test a change on your own lab

This tutorial takes a containerlab lab you already have and turns it into a test for every change. You will:

1. record a baseline of how the lab behaves today,
2. review and prune it,
3. add checks for things that must never happen,
4. make a change and run the test,
5. read the evidence when it fails,
6. run the same test in GitHub Actions.

It takes about 15 minutes. Every command and output below is from a real run (Netdryrun™ 0.3.1, containerlab 0.81.1, FRR 10.4.1, on WSL2).

## Before you start

You need Netdryrun, Docker and containerlab. See [Getting started](getting-started.md#requirements).

## 1. Your lab

Any containerlab topology works. Here, the bundled `examples/frr-bgp` lab stands in for "your lab": three FRR routers in a triangle, each in its own AS, each announcing one LAN prefix over eBGP.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun
mkdir my-lab
cp -r netdryrun/examples/frr-bgp/configs netdryrun/examples/frr-bgp/topology.clab.yml my-lab/
sed -i 's/^name: ndr-frr-bgp/name: ndr-my-lab/' my-lab/topology.clab.yml
```

The folder now holds a topology and router configs, and no `netdryrun.yml`:

```text
my-lab/
  topology.clab.yml     # name: ndr-my-lab, nodes r1 r2 r3
  configs/
    daemons  r1.conf  r2.conf  r3.conf  vtysh.conf
```

The lab name (`name:` in the topology) must be unique on the machine. See [name collisions](troubleshooting.md#a-lab-named-x-is-already-running).

## 2. Record a baseline

`netdryrun record` deploys the lab, waits for BGP to converge, writes down what it sees, and destroys the lab.

```text
$ netdryrun record my-lab/topology.clab.yml --deploy
Deploying lab ndr-my-lab, then waiting 45s for the network to converge...
recording r1 (frr)
recording r2 (frr)
recording r3 (frr)
Recorded 18 checks to /home/ndr/work/docs031/my-lab/netdryrun.yml. Review it, then: netdryrun run /home/ndr/work/docs031/my-lab
```

This took 50 seconds. The file has one check for every established BGP session, every prefix count and every BGP route. The start of it:

```yaml title="my-lab/netdryrun.yml (recorded)"
# Recorded by netdryrun 0.3.1 record on 2026-10-28T02:26:27+00:00.
# This is a baseline of the network's behavior when it was recorded. Review it before committing:
# remove anything that is allowed to change, and add negative checks (route present: false,
# ping expect: failure) for things that must never happen. Docs: https://netdryrun.com/reference/config/
lab: topology.clab.yml
timeout: 120
checks:
- type: bgp_session
  node: r1
  neighbor: 10.0.12.2
- type: bgp_prefixes
  node: r1
  neighbor: 10.0.12.2
  afi: ipv4-unicast
  exact: 2
- type: bgp_session
  node: r1
  neighbor: 10.0.13.2
# ... 15 more: the same pattern for r2 and r3, plus one route check per learned LAN
```

## 3. Review and prune it

A recorded baseline says "nothing may change". That is rarely what you want. Decide what is allowed to change.

Here is what happens if you skip this step. The change in step 5 adds a LAN on r3, and its first attempt announces it with `redistribute connected`. Run against the raw baseline, the `exact: 2` prefix counts fail, because r1 and r2 now get 6 prefixes:

```text
$ netdryrun run my-lab
Netdryrun 0.3.1: 18 checks from my-lab/netdryrun.yml
Deploying lab ndr-my-lab (3 nodes); this usually takes 30-90 s, longer the first time images are pulled...
  [PASS] r1: BGP session to 10.0.12.2 is established -- state is established (10.9s)
  ...
Convergence checks done; settling 10s before post-convergence checks...
  [FAIL] r1: prefixes from 10.0.12.2 = 2 -- 6 ipv4-unicast prefixes accepted (0.1s)
  [FAIL] r1: prefixes from 10.0.13.2 = 2 -- 6 ipv4-unicast prefixes accepted (0.1s)
  [FAIL] r2: prefixes from 10.0.12.1 = 2 -- 6 ipv4-unicast prefixes accepted (0.1s)
  [FAIL] r2: prefixes from 10.0.23.2 = 2 -- 6 ipv4-unicast prefixes accepted (0.1s)
  [PASS] r3: prefixes from 10.0.13.1 = 2 -- 2 ipv4-unicast prefixes accepted (held 10s, 5 samples) (10.1s)
  [PASS] r3: prefixes from 10.0.23.1 = 2 -- 2 ipv4-unicast prefixes accepted (held 10s, 5 samples) (10.1s)
Destroying lab...
FAILED: 14 passed, 4 failed (18 checks)
```

The test did its job: something changed. But adding a LAN is allowed, so the baseline should allow it. Edit the file:

- **Keep** every `bgp_session` check. Sessions must stay up.
- **Turn exact prefix counts into ranges.** `min: 2` keeps today's routes; `max: 10` still catches a leak that floods r1. You can also record ranges from the start with `netdryrun record --min-prefixes`.
- **Keep the route checks you care about.** This tutorial keeps r1's and removes the r2 and r3 copies to keep the file short.

## 4. Add negative checks

`record` only writes down what exists. It cannot know what must never exist. Add those checks yourself. For this lab:

- nobody sends r1 a default route,
- the point-to-point link subnets (`10.0.x.x/30`) stay out of BGP,
- and a ping, so the test proves traffic gets through, not only that routes exist.

The reviewed file:

```yaml title="my-lab/netdryrun.yml (reviewed)"
# Baseline recorded with `netdryrun record`, then reviewed by hand.
lab: topology.clab.yml
timeout: 120
checks:
# Every BGP session stays up (recorded).
- type: bgp_session
  node: r1
  neighbor: 10.0.12.2
- type: bgp_session
  node: r1
  neighbor: 10.0.13.2
- type: bgp_session
  node: r2
  neighbor: 10.0.12.1
- type: bgp_session
  node: r2
  neighbor: 10.0.23.2
- type: bgp_session
  node: r3
  neighbor: 10.0.13.1
- type: bgp_session
  node: r3
  neighbor: 10.0.23.1
# Prefix counts may grow when a site adds a LAN, but not past 10 (recorded as exact: 2, edited).
- type: bgp_prefixes
  node: r1
  neighbor: 10.0.12.2
  min: 2
  max: 10
- type: bgp_prefixes
  node: r1
  neighbor: 10.0.13.2
  min: 2
  max: 10
# Each LAN reaches the others (recorded routes; the r2 and r3 copies were removed to keep the file short).
- type: route
  node: r1
  prefix: 192.168.2.0/24
  protocol: bgp
- type: route
  node: r1
  prefix: 192.168.3.0/24
  protocol: bgp
# Added by hand: traffic gets through, not just routes.
- type: ping
  node: r1
  source: 192.168.1.1
  target: 192.168.3.1
# Added by hand: things that must never happen.
- type: route          # nobody sends r1 a default route
  node: r1
  prefix: 0.0.0.0/0
  protocol: bgp
  present: false
- type: route          # point-to-point link subnets stay out of BGP
  node: r1
  prefix: 10.0.23.0/30
  protocol: bgp
  present: false
```

Check it without starting a lab:

```text
$ netdryrun validate my-lab
OK: my-lab/netdryrun.yml (13 checks, lab /home/ndr/work/docs031/my-lab/topology.clab.yml, 3 nodes)
  - [bgp_session] r1: BGP session to 10.0.12.2 is established
  - [bgp_session] r1: BGP session to 10.0.13.2 is established
  - [bgp_session] r2: BGP session to 10.0.12.1 is established
  - [bgp_session] r2: BGP session to 10.0.23.2 is established
  - [bgp_session] r3: BGP session to 10.0.13.1 is established
  - [bgp_session] r3: BGP session to 10.0.23.1 is established
  - [bgp_prefixes] r1: prefixes from 10.0.12.2 >= 2 and <= 10
  - [bgp_prefixes] r1: prefixes from 10.0.13.2 >= 2 and <= 10
  - [route] r1: route 192.168.2.0/24 via bgp is present
  - [route] r1: route 192.168.3.0/24 via bgp is present
  - [ping] r1: ping 192.168.3.1 from 192.168.1.1 expects success
  - [route] r1: route 0.0.0.0/0 via bgp is absent
  - [route] r1: route 10.0.23.0/30 via bgp is absent
```

To check BGP attributes too (communities, AS path, local preference, MED, next hop), add `bgp_route` checks; see the [reference](reference/config.md#check-types).

Negative checks are [post-convergence checks](reference/config.md#convergence-semantics): they run after the positive checks pass and a settle time, and must hold for 10 seconds.

## 5. Make a change and run it

The change: r3 gets a second LAN, 192.168.33.0/24. A first attempt announces it with `redistribute connected`:

```diff title="configs/r3.conf (first attempt)"
 interface lo
  ip address 192.168.3.1/24
+ ip address 192.168.33.1/24
 !
@@
  address-family ipv4 unicast
   network 192.168.3.0/24
+  redistribute connected
```

Run it, and ask for the JSON and Markdown reports:

```text
$ cd my-lab
$ netdryrun run . --json report.json --markdown report.md
Netdryrun 0.3.1: 13 checks from netdryrun.yml
Deploying lab ndr-my-lab (3 nodes); this usually takes 30-90 s, longer the first time images are pulled...
  [PASS] r1: BGP session to 10.0.12.2 is established -- state is established (13.8s)
  [PASS] r1: BGP session to 10.0.13.2 is established -- state is established (13.8s)
  [PASS] r2: BGP session to 10.0.12.1 is established -- state is established (13.8s)
  [PASS] r2: BGP session to 10.0.23.2 is established -- state is established (13.8s)
  [PASS] r3: BGP session to 10.0.13.1 is established -- state is established (13.8s)
  [PASS] r3: BGP session to 10.0.23.1 is established -- state is established (13.8s)
  [PASS] r1: route 192.168.2.0/24 via bgp is present -- active via bgp (13.8s)
  [PASS] r1: route 192.168.3.0/24 via bgp is present -- active via bgp (13.8s)
  [PASS] r1: ping 192.168.3.1 from 192.168.1.1 expects success -- 3/3 replies (need 2) (13.8s)
Convergence checks done; settling 10s before post-convergence checks...
  [PASS] r1: prefixes from 10.0.12.2 >= 2 and <= 10 -- 6 ipv4-unicast prefixes accepted (held 10s, 4 samples) (10.0s)
  [PASS] r1: prefixes from 10.0.13.2 >= 2 and <= 10 -- 6 ipv4-unicast prefixes accepted (held 10s, 4 samples) (10.0s)
  [PASS] r1: route 0.0.0.0/0 via bgp is absent -- absent (held 10s, 4 samples) (10.0s)
  [FAIL] r1: route 10.0.23.0/30 via bgp is absent -- unexpectedly present via bgp (0.3s)
Destroying lab...
FAILED: 12 passed, 1 failed (13 checks)
  wrote json report: report.json
  wrote markdown report: report.md
```

The run took 41 seconds and exited with code `1`. Sessions are up, the ping works, and the prefix count is inside its range. Only the negative check caught the problem: `redistribute connected` also announces r3's link subnets.

## 6. Read the evidence

### Markdown report

`report.md` is the text the GitHub Action puts on the job page and in the PR comment. Failures come first, and each failure has the raw output of every command it ran in a collapsed block (here, the routing table and the BGP table):

````markdown title="report.md"
### ❌ Netdryrun failed

**12 passed, 1 failed** on lab ` ndr-my-lab `

| | Check | Result | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| ❌ | r1: route 10.0.23.0/30 via bgp is absent | unexpectedly present via bgp | 0.3s |
| ✅ | r1: BGP session to 10.0.12.2 is established | state is established | 13.8s |
...
| ✅ | r1: route 0.0.0.0/0 via bgp is absent | absent (held 10s, 4 samples) | 10.0s |

<details><summary>Evidence: r1: route 10.0.23.0/30 via bgp is absent</summary>

` r1$ vtysh -c show ip route 10.0.23.0/30 json `

```

````

### JSON report

`report.json` has everything ([schema](reference/cli.md#json)). The top level says what ran and where:

```json
{"schema": "netdryrun.report/v1", "status": "failed", "lab": "ndr-my-lab", "error": null, "inconclusive_reason": null,
 "summary": {"passed": 12, "failed": 1, "total": 13}}
```

`environment` records the versions and images, so a result can be reproduced:

```json
"environment": {
  "netdryrun": "0.3.1",
  "containerlab": "0.81.1",
  "python": "3.10.12",
  "host": "Linux-6.18.54.1-microsoft-standard-WSL2-x86_64-with-glibc2.35",
  "nodes": {
    "r1": {"kind": "linux", "image": "quay.io/frrouting/frr:10.4.1"},
    "r2": {"kind": "linux", "image": "quay.io/frrouting/frr:10.4.1"},
    "r3": {"kind": "linux", "image": "quay.io/frrouting/frr:10.4.1"}
  }
}
```

The failed check, with its history of samples:

```json
{
  "name": "r1: route 10.0.23.0/30 via bgp is absent",
  "type": "route",
  "params": {"node": "r1", "prefix": "10.0.23.0/30", "protocol": "bgp", "present": false},
  "passed": false,
  "detail": "unexpectedly present via bgp",
  "attempts": 1,
  "duration_s": 0.3,
  "started": "2026-10-28T02:27:55+00:00",
  "history": [{"t": 0.3, "passed": false, "detail": "unexpectedly present via bgp"}]
}
```

Its `evidence` holds the command and the full output. The interesting part: the route is selected, installed, and points at r3 (`10.0.13.2`):

```json
{
  "10.0.23.0/30":[
    {
      "prefix":"10.0.23.0/30",
      "protocol":"bgp",
      "selected":true,
      "installed":true,
      "nexthops":[
        {"ip":"10.0.13.2", "interfaceName":"eth2", "active":true}
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

(Shortened; the report keeps every field.)

To look at the routers yourself, rerun with `--keep-on-failure` and run commands with `docker exec clab-ndr-my-lab-r1 vtysh -c "..."`, then destroy the lab with the command Netdryrun prints. [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md#the-lab-never-converges-timeout) has an example.

## 7. Fix the change and run again

Announce only the new LAN, with a `network` statement:

```diff title="configs/r3.conf (fixed)"
 interface lo
  ip address 192.168.3.1/24
+ ip address 192.168.33.1/24
 !
@@
  address-family ipv4 unicast
   network 192.168.3.0/24
+  network 192.168.33.0/24
```

Add a check that the change did what it should, so the test also proves the new LAN arrives:

```yaml
# Added with the change: the new LAN reaches r1.
- type: route
  node: r1
  prefix: 192.168.33.0/24
  protocol: bgp
```

```text
$ netdryrun run . --json report.json --markdown report.md
Netdryrun 0.3.1: 14 checks from netdryrun.yml
Deploying lab ndr-my-lab (3 nodes); this usually takes 30-90 s, longer the first time images are pulled...
  [PASS] r1: BGP session to 10.0.12.2 is established -- state is established (13.9s)
  [PASS] r1: BGP session to 10.0.13.2 is established -- state is established (13.9s)
  [PASS] r2: BGP session to 10.0.12.1 is established -- state is established (13.9s)
  [PASS] r2: BGP session to 10.0.23.2 is established -- state is established (13.9s)
  [PASS] r3: BGP session to 10.0.13.1 is established -- state is established (13.9s)
  [PASS] r3: BGP session to 10.0.23.1 is established -- state is established (13.9s)
  [PASS] r1: route 192.168.2.0/24 via bgp is present -- active via bgp (13.9s)
  [PASS] r1: route 192.168.3.0/24 via bgp is present -- active via bgp (13.9s)
  [PASS] r1: ping 192.168.3.1 from 192.168.1.1 expects success -- 3/3 replies (need 2) (13.9s)
  [PASS] r1: route 192.168.33.0/24 via bgp is present -- active via bgp (13.9s)
Convergence checks done; settling 10s before post-convergence checks...
  [PASS] r1: prefixes from 10.0.12.2 >= 2 and <= 10 -- 3 ipv4-unicast prefixes accepted (held 10s, 4 samples) (10.2s)
  [PASS] r1: prefixes from 10.0.13.2 >= 2 and <= 10 -- 3 ipv4-unicast prefixes accepted (held 10s, 4 samples) (10.2s)
  [PASS] r1: route 0.0.0.0/0 via bgp is absent -- absent (held 10s, 4 samples) (10.2s)
  [PASS] r1: route 10.0.23.0/30 via bgp is absent -- absent (held 10s, 4 samples) (10.2s)
Destroying lab...
PASSED: 14 passed, 0 failed (14 checks)
  wrote json report: report.json
  wrote markdown report: report.md
```

41 seconds, exit code `0`. Commit the change and the updated `netdryrun.yml` together.

## 8. Run it on every pull request

Put the lab folder in your repository (here, `network/`) and add a workflow:

```yaml title=".github/workflows/network-dryrun.yml"
name: Network dry run
on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - "network/**"
permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write   # only for pr-comment
jobs:
  dryrun:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: netdryrun/netdryrun@v0.3.1
        with:
          path: network/
          pr-comment: true
```

Every pull request that touches `network/` now deploys the lab on the runner, runs the checks, posts the Markdown report as a comment, uploads `report.json` as an artifact, and fails if any check fails. Make the job a required status check in your branch protection to block merges on a failure.

On GitHub-hosted runners, the `frr-bgp` example's CI job (install containerlab, pull the FRR image, run its checks including a link-failure scenario; measured on 0.2.0) takes 100 to 107 seconds. Before you open a PR with untrusted contributors, read the [Action security notes](github-action.md#security-notes).

## Next

- [netdryrun.yml reference](reference/config.md): every check type, including `ping` with `expect: failure` and failure scenarios (`link_down`).
- [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md): errors you may hit and how to fix them.
- [AI agents](ai-agents.md): let an agent run the same test before it proposes a change.

Source: https://netdryrun.com/examples/

# Examples

The repository's [`examples/`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples) folder has one lab per supported network OS, a deliberately broken change, a teaching lab about leaks that ping can't see, the AI agent demo, and a Batfish-then-lab pipeline. Each folder holds a containerlab topology, the router configs and a `netdryrun.yml`.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun && cd netdryrun
netdryrun run examples/frr-bgp
```

## At a glance

Times are wall-clock for `netdryrun run` on WSL2 (20 cores, 16 GB) with images already pulled, measured on 2026-10-27 with containerlab 0.81.1 and Netdryrun™ 0.3.1, by the live layer of the 0.3.1 release check, which ran every example once on the built package ([`releases/0.3.1/gate/live.json`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/releases/0.3.1/gate/live.json) in the repository). `agent-demo` is the whole `demo.sh`, both attempts. They include deploying and destroying the lab. The first run of each example also pulls its images.

| Example | Network OS | Shows | Expected | Exit | Time |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| [frr-bgp](#frr-bgp) | FRR | Basic checks, best-path attributes, a leak guard, a link-failure scenario | `PASSED: 11 passed, 0 failed` | `0` | 99 s |
| [frr-bgp-broken](#frr-bgp-broken) | FRR | A leaked default route caught | `FAILED: 5 passed, 1 failed` | `1` | 39 s |
| [srl-frr](#srl-frr) | Nokia SR Linux + FRR | Mixed vendors | `PASSED: 7 passed, 0 failed` | `0` | 59 s |
| [srl-hidden-leak](#srl-hidden-leak) | Nokia SR Linux + FRR | A leaked default that ping, sessions and the routing table miss, on both NOSes | `PASSED: 9 passed, 0 failed`; each leak `FAILED: 8 passed, 1 failed` | `0`; `1` | 59 to 60 s |
| [sonic-frr](#sonic-frr) | SONiC VS + FRR | Configuring a NOS after boot, a port-down scenario | `PASSED: 8 passed, 0 failed` | `0` | 92 s |
| [arista-frr](#arista-frr) | Arista cEOS + FRR (your image) | A bring-your-own vendor image | `PASSED: 10 passed, 0 failed` | `0` | 97 s |
| [agent-demo](#agent-demo) `demo.sh` | FRR | An agent's leaky change rejected, the fix accepted | `Demo OK` | `0` | 70 s |
| [batfish-pipeline](#batfish-pipeline) | FRR | Batfish first, then the lab; three bad changes | `PASSED: 10 passed, 0 failed` | `0` | 100 s |

## frr-bgp

[`examples/frr-bgp`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples/frr-bgp): three FRR routers (r1, r2, r3) in a triangle, each in its own AS, each announcing one LAN over eBGP.

**Shows:** the basic check types, a negative check and a failure scenario. r1 checks both BGP sessions, a prefix count between 1 and 10 (a leak guard), a route to r3's LAN, a ping to it, the AS path and next hop of the best path to r2's LAN (a `bgp_route` check), and that no default route arrives. The scenario takes the r1-r2 link down and checks that r2's LAN is still reachable through r3, that the best path now goes through r3 (AS path `65003 65002`), and that the session over the failed link is down.

**Expected:** `PASSED: 11 passed, 0 failed (11 checks)`, exit code `0`.

This is the lab the [tutorial](tutorial.md) uses as "your lab".

To run it on every pull request, see [Test an FRR change in CI](guides/frr-ci.md).

## frr-bgp-broken

[`examples/frr-bgp-broken`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples/frr-bgp-broken): the same triangle, but r2's config (`r2-bad.conf`) adds `default-originate` toward r1.

**Shows:** a bad change being caught. Sessions are up and the ping still works, because r1 receives the leaked default route but does not select it. The negative route check fails anyway: a received-but-not-selected route counts as present.

**Expected:** `FAILED: 5 passed, 1 failed (6 checks)`, exit code `1`. The failing check:

```text
  [FAIL] r1: route 0.0.0.0/0 via bgp is absent -- unexpectedly present via bgp (not selected) (0.1s)
```

CI runs this example on every push and expects it to fail.

## srl-frr

[`examples/srl-frr`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples/srl-frr): a Nokia SR Linux router (`srl1`) peering eBGP with FRR (`frr1`).

**Shows:** a mixed-vendor lab. Both sessions, a BGP route on each side, a ping in each direction, and the best path's AS path, local preference and next hop on `srl1`. SR Linux boots slower, so the file sets `timeout: 120`.

**Expected:** `PASSED: 7 passed, 0 failed (7 checks)`, exit code `0`. The SR Linux image is about 3.2 GB.

## srl-hidden-leak

[`examples/srl-hidden-leak`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples/srl-hidden-leak): "The route leak ping can't see". SR Linux (`srl1`) and FRR (`frr1`) peer eBGP, and each has its own static default route. [`leaks/`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples/srl-hidden-leak/leaks) holds two one-line changes that each leak a default route to the peer: `default-originate` on FRR, and an export statement matching `protocol static` on SR Linux.

**Shows:** a leak that is received but never selected, because it loses to the static. Sessions, ping and the routing table look unchanged. The [README](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/examples/srl-hidden-leak/README.md) teaches how to see it by hand in each CLI (the BGP RIB on SR Linux, a `B` route without `>*` on FRR) and what happens when the static goes away. One `bgp_route` check with `present: false` per router catches each leak. Run `netdryrun run examples/srl-hidden-leak` as is, then copy a file from `leaks/` over `configs/` and run it again.

**Expected:** good configs `PASSED: 9 passed, 0 failed (9 checks)`, exit code `0`. Each leak `FAILED: 8 passed, 1 failed (9 checks)`, exit code `1`, failing only the guard on the receiving router:

```text
  [FAIL] srl1: no BGP path for 0.0.0.0/0 -- unexpectedly in the BGP table (1 path(s); as-path '65020', next hop 10.0.100.2, local-pref 100, MED 0, communities none) (2.4s)
```

Needs Netdryrun 0.3.1 or later: 0.3.0 counts `srl1`'s own static default as a BGP path, so the good configs fail. Its times in the table are from the 0.3.1 release check (the good configs and each leak, once each); the README lists earlier runs of 0.3.0 plus the fix.

## sonic-frr

[`examples/sonic-frr`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples/sonic-frr): SONiC VS (`sonic1`, the `docker-sonic-vs` image) peering eBGP with FRR (`frr1`).

**Shows:** a NOS that is configured after boot. SONiC VS has no startup config here; `setup` commands in `netdryrun.yml` wait for its services, set the interface addresses and configure BGP. Checks: the session, a route on each side, a ping, a prefix count, best-path attributes on `sonic1`, and a scenario that takes the SONiC port `Ethernet0` down and checks that the session drops and the route is withdrawn.

**Expected:** `PASSED: 8 passed, 0 failed (8 checks)`, exit code `0`. `setup` waits for SONiC's services before any check runs.

The image comes from the SONiC build server, not a registry. To get it and run the lab on every pull request, see [Test a SONiC change in CI](guides/sonic-ci.md).

## arista-frr

[`examples/arista-frr`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples/arista-frr): an Arista cEOS router (`ceos1`) peering eBGP with FRR (`frr1`).

**Shows:** a vendor image you bring yourself. cEOS-lab is free from arista.com with an account but can't be redistributed, so import it as `ceos:4.36.3M` first (the comment in `topology.clab.yml` shows how). Checks: both sessions, a prefix count, a route on each side, a ping, best-path attributes on `ceos1`, no default route at the Arista, and a scenario that takes the link down from the FRR side.

**Expected:** `PASSED: 10 passed, 0 failed (10 checks)`, exit code `0`. Without the image, the run stops with exit code `2`; see [the cEOS image is missing](troubleshooting.md#the-ceos-image-is-missing).

## agent-demo

[`examples/agent-demo`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples/agent-demo): an edge router (`edge1`, AS 65000) with a customer, an upstream and a peer, a ticket ([`TICKET.md`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/examples/agent-demo/TICKET.md)) and the network team's 14 checks, including route-leak guards.

**Shows:** how an AI agent's change is judged. `demo.sh` replays two hand-written attempts: removing the prefix-list filters (passes the ticket checks, fails the leak guards) and adding the new block to two prefix lists (passes everything). See [AI agents](ai-agents.md#demo-a-ticket-a-tempting-change-a-verdict) and the [real agent run](ai-agents.md#a-real-agent-run).

**Expected:**

- `examples/agent-demo/demo.sh` exits `0` and ends with:

    ```text
    Demo OK: attempt 1 rejected by 5 leak guards with every other check passing; attempt 2 passed every check.
    ```

    Attempt 1 ends `FAILED: 9 passed, 5 failed (14 checks)`, attempt 2 `PASSED: 14 passed, 0 failed (14 checks)`. The two runs together took about 70 s (0.3.1 release check).

- `netdryrun run examples/agent-demo` shows the starting point, before anyone has worked the ticket: the guards pass and the 3 ticket checks fail, `FAILED: 11 passed, 3 failed (14 checks)`, exit code `1`. It took 119 seconds, because the failing ticket checks wait for their timeout.

## batfish-pipeline

[`examples/batfish-pipeline`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples/batfish-pipeline): the `frr-bgp` triangle behind a two-stage gate. `pipeline.sh` runs Batfish on the configs first (nothing boots), then the lab. It needs a running Batfish service and `pybatfish`.

**Shows:** what each stage catches. Three changes to r2 are in `changes/`: a leaked default route and a route-map typo (Batfish fails them in 2 to 3 seconds of analysis) and a switch to FRR's `traditional` defaults, which Batfish passes but the lab fails. See [Batfish, then Netdryrun](batfish.md) for the measured results.

**Expected:** `pipeline.sh` with no change: Batfish `8 passed, 0 failed`, then `PASSED: 10 passed, 0 failed (10 checks)`, exit code `0`. The time in the table includes both stages, with the Batfish service already running.

## Use an example as a template

Copy a folder, change `name:` in `topology.clab.yml` (lab names must be unique on the machine), replace the configs with yours, and edit the checks. Or start from your own topology with `netdryrun record`, as in the [tutorial](tutorial.md).


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/guides/frr-ci/

# Test an FRR change in CI

You keep FRR configs in git, one `frr.conf` per router. This guide makes every pull request that touches them boot the routers in containerlab with the changed configs, check how they route, and fail the job if something broke. It uses [`examples/frr-bgp`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples/frr-bgp) and its broken twin [`examples/frr-bgp-broken`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples/frr-bgp-broken); every output below is from a real run.

## 1. The lab: one folder next to your configs

`examples/frr-bgp` is three FRR routers in a triangle, each in its own AS, each announcing one LAN over eBGP. The folder holds:

```text
frr-bgp/
  topology.clab.yml      containerlab topology
  configs/r1.conf        one frr.conf per router (r2.conf, r3.conf)
  configs/daemons        which FRR daemons start
  configs/vtysh.conf     one line: service integrated-vtysh-config
  netdryrun.yml          the checks
```

Each router is a plain `linux` node running the FRR image, with the three files bind-mounted where FRR expects them:

```yaml title="topology.clab.yml"
name: ndr-frr-bgp

topology:
  defaults:
    kind: linux
    image: quay.io/frrouting/frr:10.4.1
  nodes:
    r1:
      binds:
        - configs/daemons:/etc/frr/daemons
        - configs/vtysh.conf:/etc/frr/vtysh.conf
        - configs/r1.conf:/etc/frr/frr.conf
    # r2 and r3 the same, with their own frr.conf
  links:
    - endpoints: ["r1:eth1", "r2:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["r2:eth2", "r3:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["r3:eth2", "r1:eth2"]
```

FRR details that matter here:

- **`daemons` decides what runs.** `bgpd=yes` (and `staticd=yes` for static routes) or BGP never starts. Netdryrun then reports the run as `inconclusive` (exit code `3`), not as a failed change, because no node ever returned BGP state.
- **`vtysh.conf` with `service integrated-vtysh-config`** makes `vtysh` read the single `frr.conf`, which is the file your pull request changes.
- **`eth0` is containerlab's management interface.** Your links start at `eth1`, and `frr.conf` should name those.
- **Pin the image** to the FRR version you run, not `latest`. Behavior and defaults change between releases.

## 2. The checks that matter for FRR

```yaml title="netdryrun.yml"
lab: topology.clab.yml
timeout: 90   # seconds each positive check may wait for convergence

checks:
  - type: bgp_session
    node: r1
    neighbor: 10.0.12.2
  - type: bgp_session
    node: r1
    neighbor: 10.0.13.2
  - type: bgp_prefixes
    node: r1
    neighbor: 10.0.12.2
    min: 1
    max: 10          # guards against a route leak flooding r1
  - type: route
    node: r1
    prefix: 192.168.3.0/24
    protocol: bgp
  - type: ping
    node: r1
    source: 192.168.1.1
    target: 192.168.3.1
  - type: bgp_route    # r1 prefers r2's direct path to r2's LAN over the longer path via r3
    node: r1
    prefix: 192.168.2.0/24
    as_path: "65002"
    next_hop: 10.0.12.2
  - type: route        # nothing should send r1 a default route
    node: r1
    prefix: 0.0.0.0/0
    protocol: bgp
    present: false

scenarios:
  - name: r1-r2 link fails
    link_down: {node: r1, interface: eth1}
    checks:
      - type: route        # r2's LAN is still reachable, now via r3
        node: r1
        prefix: 192.168.2.0/24
        protocol: bgp
      - type: bgp_route    # the best path now goes the long way, through r3
        node: r1
        prefix: 192.168.2.0/24
        as_path: "65003 65002"
        next_hop: 10.0.13.2
      - type: ping
        node: r1
        source: 192.168.1.1
        target: 192.168.2.1
      - type: bgp_session  # and the session over the failed link is really down
        node: r1
        neighbor: 10.0.12.2
        state: down        # any state except established
```

On FRR, each check type reads a different part of the router, and the differences are where changes go wrong:

| Check | Reads | Why it matters on FRR |
|---|---|---|
| `bgp_session` | `show bgp neighbors json` | An `Established` session can still carry nothing. Never use it alone |
| `bgp_prefixes` | `acceptedPrefixCounter` in `show bgp neighbors json` | Counts prefixes after your inbound policy. A filter that drops everything shows here first. `max` is a cheap leak guard |
| `route` | `show ip route <prefix> json` (zebra) | Selected and installed. zebra keeps the losing entries too, so `present: false` also fails on a route that was received but lost |
| `bgp_route` | `show bgp ipv4 unicast <prefix> json` (bgpd) | The best path's AS path, next hop, local preference, MED, communities. Catches a change that still delivers the route, but the long way |
| `ping` | `ping -I <source>` in the container | The data plane, from the source address you give |

BGP's best path and zebra's selected route are not the same thing. A default route leaked by a peer is `*>` (best) in `show bgp ipv4 unicast`, because the static it loses to isn't a BGP path, and it is not selected in `show ip route`. Read the table that answers your question: `bgp_route` for "which path does BGP prefer", `route` for "what does the router forward with". The [hidden leak lab](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples/srl-hidden-leak) shows both side by side.

## 3. Run it locally

```bash
pip install netdryrun
netdryrun run examples/frr-bgp
```

```text
Netdryrun 0.3.1: 7 checks from examples/frr-bgp/netdryrun.yml
Deploying lab ndr-frr-bgp (3 nodes); this usually takes 30-90 s, longer the first time images are pulled...
  [PASS] r1: BGP session to 10.0.12.2 is established -- state is established (13.5s)
  [PASS] r1: BGP session to 10.0.13.2 is established -- state is established (13.5s)
  [PASS] r1: route 192.168.3.0/24 via bgp is present -- active via bgp (13.5s)
  [PASS] r1: ping 192.168.3.1 from 192.168.1.1 expects success -- 3/3 replies (need 2) (13.5s)
Convergence checks done; settling 10s before post-convergence checks...
  [PASS] r1: prefixes from 10.0.12.2 >= 1 and <= 10 -- 2 ipv4-unicast prefixes accepted (held 10s, 4 samples) (10.3s)
  [PASS] r1: BGP best path for 192.168.2.0/24 has as-path '65002', next hop 10.0.12.2 -- best path: as-path '65002', next hop 10.0.12.2, local-pref 100, MED 0, communities none (held 10s, 4 samples) (10.3s)
  [PASS] r1: route 0.0.0.0/0 via bgp is absent -- absent (held 10s, 4 samples) (10.3s)
Scenario: r1-r2 link fails
  the fault took effect after 0s (2 BGP session(s) over the downed links are down)
  settling 10s before the scenario's checks
  [PASS] [r1-r2 link fails] r1: route 192.168.2.0/24 via bgp is present -- active via bgp (held 12s, 3 samples) (19.4s)
  [PASS] [r1-r2 link fails] r1: ping 192.168.2.1 from 192.168.1.1 expects success -- 3/3 replies (need 2) (held 12s, 3 samples) (19.4s)
  [PASS] [r1-r2 link fails] r1: BGP best path for 192.168.2.0/24 has as-path '65003 65002', next hop 10.0.13.2 -- best path: as-path '65003 65002', next hop 10.0.13.2, local-pref 100, MED 0, communities none (held 10s, 4 samples) (10.0s)
  [PASS] [r1-r2 link fails] r1: BGP session to 10.0.12.2 is down -- state is active (held 10s, 4 samples) (10.0s)
Restored 1 link(s) and 0 route injection(s); settling 10s
Destroying lab...
PASSED: 11 passed, 0 failed (11 checks)
```

The `bgp_route` checks run with the post-convergence checks and must hold for 10 seconds, because the best path can change when a slower session comes up. In the scenario, Netdryrun first waits until both ends of the BGP session over the downed link see it down (here at once, because the interface itself went down), settles 10 seconds, and then the positive checks must keep passing for the hold window, not just once. See [scenario timing](../reference/config.md#scenario-timing).

Now the broken change. `frr-bgp-broken` is the same triangle, but r2's config adds one line, `neighbor 10.0.12.1 default-originate`, toward r1:

```bash
netdryrun run examples/frr-bgp-broken
```

```text
Netdryrun 0.3.1: 6 checks from examples/frr-bgp-broken/netdryrun.yml
Deploying lab ndr-frr-broken (3 nodes); this usually takes 30-90 s, longer the first time images are pulled...
  [PASS] r1: BGP session to 10.0.12.2 is established -- state is established (13.5s)
  [PASS] r1: BGP session to 10.0.13.2 is established -- state is established (13.5s)
  [PASS] r1: route 192.168.3.0/24 via bgp is present -- active via bgp (13.5s)
  [PASS] r1: ping 192.168.3.1 from 192.168.1.1 expects success -- 3/3 replies (need 2) (13.5s)
Convergence checks done; settling 10s before post-convergence checks...
  [PASS] r1: prefixes from 10.0.12.2 >= 1 and <= 10 -- 3 ipv4-unicast prefixes accepted (held 10s, 5 samples) (10.1s)
  [FAIL] r1: route 0.0.0.0/0 via bgp is absent -- unexpectedly present via bgp (not selected) (0.2s)
Destroying lab...
FAILED: 5 passed, 1 failed (6 checks)
```

Sessions are up, the prefix count is within its limit, and the ping works: the LANs have more specific routes, so a default route changes nothing for them. r1 doesn't even select the leaked default, because in this lab it loses to containerlab's management default route (see [Gotchas](#gotchas)). The `present: false` check fails anyway, because zebra still holds the losing BGP entry, and the run exits with `1`.

## 4. Run it on every pull request

```yaml title=".github/workflows/network-dryrun.yml"
name: Network dry run
on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - "network/**"
permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write   # for pr-comment
jobs:
  dryrun:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: netdryrun/netdryrun@v0.3.1
        with:
          path: network/        # the folder with netdryrun.yml
          pr-comment: true
```

The job installs containerlab and Netdryrun, pulls the FRR image, runs the checks, uploads the JSON and JUnit reports, and fails if a check fails. With `pr-comment: true` it also posts the verdict and the evidence for each failed check on the pull request. See [GitHub Action](../github-action.md) for every input, and the security notes before running labs from forks.

**Other CI systems:** any Linux runner that can start privileged Docker containers works. The steps are the same three commands. `env "PATH=$PATH"` keeps the `netdryrun` that `pip` installed on the path under `sudo`:

```bash
bash -c "$(curl -sL https://get.containerlab.dev)" -- -v 0.81.1
pip install netdryrun
sudo env "PATH=$PATH" netdryrun run network/ --junit netdryrun-junit.xml --json netdryrun-report.json
```

Exit codes: `0` passed, `1` a check failed, `2` a setup problem (bad YAML, the lab didn't start), `3` inconclusive (the lab never reached a testable state; rerun it).

## Times

Wall-clock for `netdryrun run`, including deploying and destroying the lab, with images already pulled. Measured on 2026-10-28 on WSL2 (20 cores, 16 GB), containerlab 0.81.1, Netdryrun 0.3.1 installed from PyPI, running the two example folders of a fresh clone:

| Run | Result | Exit | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| `examples/frr-bgp` (7 checks and a link-failure scenario) | `PASSED: 11 passed, 0 failed` | `0` | 105 s |
| `examples/frr-bgp-broken` | `FAILED: 5 passed, 1 failed` | `1` | 41 s |

The failing run is shorter because it has no failure scenario. `frr-bgp` takes longer than on 0.3.0 (88 s) because 0.3.1 settles 10 s after the fault and holds the scenario's checks for a full window, instead of judging them as soon as they pass. The [examples page](../examples.md) shows 99 s and 39 s for the same two labs from the 0.3.1 release check on the same machine the day before; runs differ by several seconds. On GitHub-hosted `ubuntu-latest` runners, the whole job (installing containerlab and Netdryrun, pulling FRR, running) took 100 to 107 s for `frr-bgp` and 54 to 66 s for `frr-bgp-broken`, over three CI runs on `main` on 2026-10-27, before the 0.3.0 release added a `bgp_route` check to `frr-bgp`; see [the FAQ](../faq.md#how-long-does-a-run-take-and-what-does-ci-cost). On a private repository, jobs are billed by the minute, rounded up: the `frr-bgp` job uses 2.

## Gotchas

- **eBGP without a policy may exchange nothing.** Under FRR's default `traditional` profile, `bgp ebgp-requires-policy` is on (RFC 8212): an eBGP neighbor with no route-map in or out reaches `Established` and accepts and sends nothing. Under `frr defaults datacenter`, which the examples use, it's off. On FRR 10.4.1 with no route-maps, the `traditional` side shows:

    ```text
    Neighbor        V         AS   MsgRcvd   MsgSent   TblVer  InQ OutQ  Up/Down State/PfxRcd   PfxSnt Desc
    10.9.0.2        4      65002        12        11        1    0    0 00:00:24     (Policy) (Policy) FRRouting/10.4.1_git
    ```

    A `bgp_session` check passes either way; `bgp_prefixes` and `route` checks catch it. Keep the same `frr defaults` line in the lab as in production.
- **containerlab gives `linux` nodes a default route** via the management network. FRR sees it as a kernel route with distance 0, which beats a static or BGP default. If your change or your checks involve the default route, delete it with `exec: ["ip route del default"]` on the node, as the [hidden leak lab](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples/srl-hidden-leak) does.
- **Lab names are global on a machine.** Two jobs on one self-hosted runner, or two copies of a folder, must use different `name:` values in `topology.clab.yml`.
- **`frr.conf` is read at boot.** Netdryrun deploys a fresh lab on every run, so the pull request's file is always the one tested. If you poke at a lab kept with `--keep`, changes you make in `vtysh` are not in the file.


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/guides/sonic-ci/

# Test a SONiC change in CI

SONiC is different from most network OSes in a lab: the virtual switch image boots with no configuration, and its services come up one by one after the container starts. This guide shows how to get the image, configure the switch once it's ready, and check its routing on every pull request. It uses [`examples/sonic-frr`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples/sonic-frr): a SONiC VS switch peering eBGP with an FRR router. Every output below is from a real run.

## 1. Get the image

`docker-sonic-vs` is the virtual switch the SONiC project builds for its own tests. It is not on a container registry: the SONiC build server publishes it as a compressed file. Download it and load it into Docker:

```bash
curl -L -o docker-sonic-vs.gz \
  "https://sonic-build.azurewebsites.net/api/sonic/artifacts?branchName=master&platform=vs&target=target/docker-sonic-vs.gz"
docker load -i docker-sonic-vs.gz      # creates docker-sonic-vs:latest
```

The file is about 230 MB (232,075,139 bytes for the build used on this page, downloaded on 2026-10-27). Loaded, the image is 1.92 GB.

`branchName=master` is the latest build, so it changes over time. For repeatable CI, keep the file you tested with (as a release asset or in a cache) instead of downloading `master` on every run.

## 2. The lab

```yaml title="topology.clab.yml"
name: ndr-sonic-frr

topology:
  nodes:
    sonic1:
      kind: sonic-vs
      image: docker-sonic-vs:latest
    frr1:
      kind: linux
      image: quay.io/frrouting/frr:10.4.1
      binds:
        - configs/daemons:/etc/frr/daemons
        - configs/vtysh.conf:/etc/frr/vtysh.conf
        - configs/frr1.conf:/etc/frr/frr.conf
  links:
    - endpoints: ["sonic1:eth1", "frr1:eth1"]
```

In `kind: sonic-vs`, the container's `eth1` is the SONiC port `Ethernet0`. The topology names `eth1`; SONiC commands and checks use `Ethernet0`.

## 3. Configure SONiC after boot: `setup`

There's no startup config. Instead, `netdryrun.yml` lists `setup` commands that Netdryrun runs inside the node after deploying the lab and before any check:

```yaml title="netdryrun.yml"
lab: topology.clab.yml
timeout: 180

nodes:
  sonic1:
    setup:
      - supervisorctl status orchagent | grep -q RUNNING && supervisorctl status bgpd | grep -q RUNNING
      - config interface ip add Ethernet0 10.0.40.1/30 && config interface startup Ethernet0
      - config loopback add Loopback0; config interface ip add Loopback0 192.168.40.1/32
      - >-
        vtysh -c "conf t" -c "router bgp 65040" -c "bgp router-id 40.40.40.40" -c "no bgp ebgp-requires-policy"
        -c "neighbor 10.0.40.2 remote-as 65020" -c "address-family ipv4 unicast" -c "network 192.168.40.1/32"
```

Line by line:

1. **Wait for the services.** The container is "running" long before SONiC is. `orchagent` (which programs the switch) and `bgpd` (FRR inside SONiC) have to be `RUNNING` before `config` commands and `vtysh` work. This line fails until they are.
2. **Address and enable the port** with SONiC's `config` CLI, which writes to CONFIG_DB like on a real switch.
3. **A loopback** for the announced prefix.
4. **BGP**, configured in the FRR that runs inside SONiC, through `vtysh`.

Each line is retried every 5 seconds until it succeeds, within a shared budget of 300 seconds. A line runs again from the start if any part of it fails, so put the part that can fail first (as line 1 does), and keep lines that change state safe to run twice.

## 4. The checks that matter for SONiC

```yaml
checks:
  - type: bgp_session
    node: sonic1
    neighbor: 10.0.40.2
  - type: route
    node: sonic1
    prefix: 192.168.20.0/24
    protocol: bgp
  - type: route
    node: frr1
    prefix: 192.168.40.1/32
    protocol: bgp
  - type: ping
    node: sonic1
    source: 192.168.40.1
    target: 192.168.20.1
  - type: bgp_prefixes
    node: frr1
    neighbor: 10.0.40.1
    min: 1
    max: 5
  - type: bgp_route
    node: sonic1
    prefix: 192.168.20.0/24
    as_path: "65020"
    local_pref: 100
    next_hop: 10.0.40.2

scenarios:
  - name: SONiC port Ethernet0 goes down
    link_down: {node: sonic1, interface: Ethernet0}
    checks:
      - {type: bgp_session, node: frr1, neighbor: 10.0.40.1, state: down}
      - {type: route, node: frr1, prefix: 192.168.40.1/32, protocol: bgp, present: false}
```

What to know about these on SONiC:

- **Routing state comes from the FRR inside SONiC.** The `sonic` driver reads sessions, routes and BGP paths through `vtysh`, exactly as on FRR. A route check says what SONiC's routing stack selected. It does not read what `orchagent` programmed (APPL_DB, ASIC_DB).
- **`ping` covers the data path.** It runs from the switch with the loopback as source, so it only passes if the port, its address and the route all work. Keep at least one ping per change.
- **Check from the other side too.** `route` and `bgp_prefixes` on `frr1` prove what SONiC actually announces, which is what a policy change on the switch affects.
- **A port-down scenario uses the SONiC name.** `link_down` on `Ethernet0` takes the port down inside the switch. The scenario then checks that the peer sees the session drop and the route withdrawn, and Netdryrun brings the port back afterwards.
- **Give it time.** `timeout: 180` covers the slow boot; the `setup` budget is separate.

## 5. Run it locally

```bash
pip install netdryrun
netdryrun run examples/sonic-frr
```

```text
Netdryrun 0.3.1: 6 checks from examples/sonic-frr/netdryrun.yml
Deploying lab ndr-sonic-frr (2 nodes); this usually takes 30-90 s, longer the first time images are pulled...
Running setup on sonic1...
setup done on sonic1 (4 commands)
  [PASS] sonic1: BGP session to 10.0.40.2 is established -- state is established (13.7s)
  [PASS] sonic1: route 192.168.20.0/24 via bgp is present -- active via bgp (13.7s)
  [PASS] frr1: route 192.168.40.1/32 via bgp is present -- active via bgp (13.7s)
  [PASS] sonic1: ping 192.168.20.1 from 192.168.40.1 expects success -- 3/3 replies (need 2) (13.7s)
Convergence checks done; settling 10s before post-convergence checks...
  [PASS] frr1: prefixes from 10.0.40.1 >= 1 and <= 5 -- 1 ipv4-unicast prefixes accepted (held 10s, 5 samples) (10.2s)
  [PASS] sonic1: BGP best path for 192.168.20.0/24 has as-path '65020', local-pref 100, next hop 10.0.40.2 -- best path: as-path '65020', next hop 10.0.40.2, local-pref 100, MED 0, communities none (held 10s, 5 samples) (10.2s)
Scenario: SONiC port Ethernet0 goes down
  the fault took effect after 0s (1 BGP session(s) over the downed links are down)
  settling 10s before the scenario's checks
  [PASS] [SONiC port Ethernet0 goes down] frr1: BGP session to 10.0.40.1 is down -- state is connect (held 10s, 4 samples) (10.1s)
  [PASS] [SONiC port Ethernet0 goes down] frr1: route 192.168.40.1/32 via bgp is absent -- absent (held 10s, 4 samples) (10.1s)
Restored 1 link(s) and 0 route injection(s); settling 10s
Destroying lab...
PASSED: 8 passed, 0 failed (8 checks)
```

## 6. Run it on every pull request

The workflow is the usual one with one extra step: load the image before Netdryrun deploys the lab. containerlab only pulls images that are missing, so the loaded `docker-sonic-vs:latest` is used as is.

```yaml title=".github/workflows/sonic-dryrun.yml"
name: SONiC dry run
on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - "network/sonic/**"
jobs:
  dryrun:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Load docker-sonic-vs
        run: |
          curl -fsSL -o docker-sonic-vs.gz \
            "https://sonic-build.azurewebsites.net/api/sonic/artifacts?branchName=master&platform=vs&target=target/docker-sonic-vs.gz"
          docker load -i docker-sonic-vs.gz
      - uses: netdryrun/netdryrun@v0.3.1
        with:
          path: network/sonic/
```

On other CI systems: load the image the same way, then install containerlab and Netdryrun and run `sudo env "PATH=$PATH" netdryrun run <folder>`, as in the [FRR guide](frr-ci.md#4-run-it-on-every-pull-request).

This workflow is a recipe, not something Netdryrun's own CI runs yet: SONiC isn't in the project's CI, and the workflow hasn't been run on a hosted runner. The runs on this page are local.

## Times

Wall-clock for `netdryrun run`, including deploying the lab, the `setup` lines, the checks, the port-down scenario and destroying the lab, with both images already loaded. Measured on 2026-10-28 on WSL2 (20 cores, 16 GB), containerlab 0.81.1, Netdryrun 0.3.1 installed from PyPI, running the example folder of a fresh clone:

| Run | Result | Exit | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| `examples/sonic-frr` (6 checks and a port-down scenario) | `PASSED: 8 passed, 0 failed` | `0` | 99 s |

The positive checks passed 13.7 s after `setup` finished. The [examples page](../examples.md) shows 92 s from the 0.3.1 release check on the same machine the day before; runs differ by a few seconds. In CI, add the time to download the 230 MB image, which depends on the runner's network; caching the file avoids it.

## Gotchas

- **"Running" isn't ready.** The container is up long before SONiC's services are, and `config` and `vtysh` don't work until they are. Make the first `setup` line a readiness check, so every later line starts on a ready switch.
- **`no bgp ebgp-requires-policy`.** With it on (RFC 8212, FRR's default profile), an eBGP neighbor with no route-map comes up and exchanges nothing; see the [FRR guide's gotchas](frr-ci.md#gotchas). The example turns it off to stay short. With real policies, attach route-maps instead.
- **The image is big and not on a registry.** About 230 MB to download and 1.92 GB once loaded. Cache it in CI.
- **Port names differ between the topology and the switch:** `eth1` in `topology.clab.yml`, `Ethernet0` in SONiC commands, checks and scenarios.
- **Memory:** about 300 MiB for the SONiC VS node once up ([FAQ](../faq.md#how-much-memory-and-cpu-does-it-need)).


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/reference/config/

# netdryrun.yml reference

`netdryrun.yml` describes one lab and the behavior you expect from it. Commands accept either the file or the folder that contains it (`netdryrun run network/` reads `network/netdryrun.yml`).

```yaml title="netdryrun.yml"
lab: topology.clab.yml
timeout: 90
nodes:
  r1:
    driver: frr
checks:
  - type: bgp_session
    node: r1
    neighbor: 10.0.12.2
  - type: route
    node: r1
    prefix: 0.0.0.0/0
    protocol: bgp
    present: false
```

Validation is strict, and every problem is an error (exit code `2`) before anything is deployed. Run `netdryrun validate` to check a file without starting a lab. From 0.3.1:

- **Unknown keys are errors at every level**: the top level, `nodes.<node>`, checks, scenarios, `link_down`, `node_isolated` and `inject_routes`. A misspelled key gets a suggestion: `unknown keys ['presnt'] for type route; did you mean 'present'?`. Before 0.3.1, a misspelled key at the top level, under `nodes` or inside a fault was ignored, so a misspelled block of checks never ran (keys inside a check or a scenario were already refused).
- **Duplicate keys are errors**, at any depth: `duplicate key 'present' (first defined on line 12)`. Plain YAML keeps the last one silently. The topology file is read the same way. YAML merge keys (`<<: *anchor`) are allowed.
- **Malformed YAML** is reported on one line, with its position: `netdryrun.yml: not valid YAML at line 7, column 3: ...`.
- **Booleans must be real booleans**: `present` and `active` take unquoted `true` or `false`. A quoted `"false"`, `0`, `null` or an empty value is refused instead of being read as something else.
- **Values come from fixed lists** where the drivers only understand certain values: `type`, `state`, `afi`, `protocol`, `expect` and `nodes.<node>.driver`. A near miss gets a suggestion (`afi: ipv4` → `did you mean 'ipv4-unicast'?`).
- **Numbers are range-checked**: see the tables below. Required keys missing, IP addresses that don't parse, and keys that make no sense together (`min_replies` with `expect: failure`, `hold` on a check where it has no effect) are errors too.

## Top-level keys

| Key | Required | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `lab` | yes | | Path to the containerlab topology file, relative to `netdryrun.yml`. The topology must have a `name`. |
| `timeout` | no | `120` | Seconds a check may wait (see [convergence semantics](#convergence-semantics)). A positive number, at most `86400`. Each check can override it. |
| `checks` | yes | | List of checks. At least one is required. |
| `nodes` | no | | A mapping of node name to settings. Each node accepts only `driver` and `setup`. |
| `nodes.<node>.driver` | no | detected | Force the driver for a node: `frr`, `srlinux`, `eos` or `sonic`. See [drivers](#drivers). |
| `nodes.<node>.setup` | no | | Shell commands run inside the node after deploy, before any check. Each is retried every 5 s until it succeeds (the NOS may still be booting), within a shared 300 s budget. For NOSes that are configured after boot, such as SONiC. |
| `scenarios` | no | | A non-empty list of [failure scenarios](#failure-scenarios). |

No other top-level key is accepted.

## Keys every check accepts

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `type` | required | `bgp_session`, `bgp_prefixes`, `route`, `bgp_route` or `ping` |
| `node` | required | Node name from the topology (for example `r1`) |
| `name` | generated | Label used in reports. The default describes the check, for example `r1: BGP session to 10.0.12.2 is established`. |
| `timeout` | top-level `timeout` | Seconds this check may wait to pass. A positive number, at most `86400`. |
| `hold` | `--hold` (10) | Seconds a [post-convergence check](#convergence-semantics) must hold. A positive number, at most `86400`. Only allowed on post-convergence checks: on any other check it would have no effect, so it is an error. |
| `vrf` | `default` | VRF (FRR, SONiC, Arista EOS) or network-instance (SR Linux) to look in. Letters, digits and `. _ : -`, at most 64 characters: the name goes into the device's CLI command, so anything else is refused (0.3.1 and later; 0.3.0 did not check it). `vrf: all` is refused: name one VRF per check. A VRF that doesn't exist on the node is an error on every driver, never "no routes" (see [drivers](#drivers)). |

Each check type accepts only these keys and the ones in its own table.

IP addresses and prefixes are normalized, so `2001:db8:0::1` in YAML matches `2001:db8::1` on the device. Prefixes with host bits set are reduced to the network (`10.0.0.1/24` becomes `10.0.0.0/24`).

## Check types

### bgp_session

A BGP session reaches a state.

| Key | Required | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `neighbor` | yes | | Neighbor IP address as configured on `node` |
| `state` | no | `established` | One of `idle`, `connect`, `active`, `opensent`, `openconfirm`, `established`, or `down` (any state except established). Case-insensitive |

The check fails if the neighbor is not configured. A `state` other than `established` makes it a post-convergence check.

```yaml
- type: bgp_session
  node: r1
  neighbor: 10.0.12.2
```

### bgp_prefixes

The number of prefixes accepted from a neighbor is within a range. Accepted means received minus rejected by import policy.

| Key | Required | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `neighbor` | yes | | Neighbor IP address |
| `min` | one of `min`, `max`, `exact` | | Lower bound, inclusive |
| `max` | one of `min`, `max`, `exact` | | Upper bound, inclusive |
| `exact` | one of `min`, `max`, `exact` | | Exact count |
| `afi` | no | `ipv4-unicast` | Address family: exactly one of `ipv4-unicast`, `ipv6-unicast` or `evpn` (case-insensitive). `evpn` is supported on FRR and SONiC only, not on SR Linux or Arista EOS |

Rules:

- At least one of `min`, `max` or `exact` is required.
- `exact` cannot be combined with `min` or `max`.
- `min` must not be greater than `max`.
- All three are non-negative integers.
- `min: 0` on its own is refused: it always passes. Use `min: 1` or more, or add `max`.
- Any other `afi` is refused (from 0.3.1). An address family the drivers don't report would read as 0 prefixes, which passes `max` and `exact: 0`.
- `afi: evpn` on an SR Linux or Arista EOS node is refused before the lab deploys (exit code `2`): those drivers read only the IPv4 and IPv6 unicast counts (SR Linux has no received-routes counter for EVPN), so an EVPN count would always read 0. SR Linux refuses it from 0.3.1; before, the count read 0 and passed `max`.
- The session must be `established`. Counters reset to 0 when a session drops, so a count from a down session would satisfy `max` by accident; Netdryrun fails the check instead.
- If the session is established but the address family reports nothing, the count is 0.
- A check with `max` or `exact` is a post-convergence check. A check with only `min` is a positive check.

```yaml
- type: bgp_prefixes
  node: r1
  neighbor: 10.0.12.2
  min: 1
  max: 10          # guards against a route leak flooding r1
```

### route

A route is present in (or absent from) the routing table.

| Key | Required | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `prefix` | yes | | IPv4 or IPv6 prefix |
| `present` | no | `true` | `false` means the route must be absent. Unquoted `true` or `false` only |
| `protocol` | no | any | Only count routes from this protocol: one of the names in [protocol names](#protocol-names). Case-insensitive |
| `vrf` | no | `default` | VRF or network-instance |
| `active` | no | `true` | With `present: true`: `false` also accepts a route that is in the table but not selected (for example a BGP default losing to a local one). Unquoted `true` or `false` only; not allowed with `present: false` |

- **Present** means an *active* route matches: selected and installed on FRR, `active` on SR Linux.
- **Absent** means no matching route at all, active or not. A BGP path that was received from a neighbor still counts as present, valid or not, selected or not (for example a leaked default losing to a local one), so `present: false` fails. This is how the [failing example](../index.md#a-failing-run) is caught. Every driver reads the BGP table for this as well as the routing table; there, only paths received from a neighbor count, not the router's own (network statements, redistribution, SR Linux's static and interface routes).
- `protocol` must be a name the drivers report. `ebgp` and `ibgp` are refused: drivers report both as `bgp`. A name outside the list would match nothing and silently pass `present: false`.
- `present: false` makes it a post-convergence check.

```yaml
- type: route
  node: r1
  prefix: 192.168.3.0/24
  protocol: bgp
```

### bgp_route

Attributes of the BGP **best path** for a prefix: communities, AS path, local preference, MED, next hop. Many real policy bugs live here: a route that is still present but lost its community, got the wrong local preference, or now goes the long way. `route` reads the routing table; `bgp_route` reads the BGP table.

| Key | Required | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `prefix` | yes | | IPv4 or IPv6 prefix, matched exactly |
| `communities` | no | | The best path must carry **all** of these. Standard (`'65000:100'`), large (`'65000:1:2'`) or well-known names (`no-export`, `no-advertise`, `no-peer`, `blackhole`, `graceful-shutdown`, `accept-own`, `llgr-stale`, `no-llgr`, `no-export-subconfed`) |
| `without_communities` | no | | The best path must carry **none** of these. Same forms as `communities` |
| `as_path` | no | | Exact AS path, ASNs separated by spaces: `"65002 65003"`. `""` is the empty path of a locally originated route. AS sets are written `{65004,65005}` |
| `as_path_regex` | no | | Python regular expression searched in the AS path string, for example `"^65002 "` (learned from 65002) or `"(^| )65666( |$)"` (passes through 65666). It runs with no time limit, so avoid nested repeats such as `(\d+ ?)+$` that can backtrack for minutes |
| `local_pref` | no | | Exact local preference |
| `med` | no | | Exact MED. A path without MED counts as `0`, as best-path selection treats it by default |
| `next_hop` | no | | Exact next hop address |
| `present` | no | `true` | `false` means no path at all for the prefix in the BGP table, best or not, valid or not. Unquoted `true` or `false` only |
| `vrf` | no | `default` | VRF or network-instance |

Rules:

- Without attribute keys, the check passes when a best path exists.
- **Quote communities.** YAML reads some unquoted values as numbers (`65000:10` is a base-60 number to YAML 1.1), so an unquoted community that YAML turns into a number is a config error.
- A community can't be in both `communities` and `without_communities`.
- `present: false` can't be combined with attribute keys. To forbid a community on the best path, use `without_communities`.
- The check fails if there is no path, or no best path (for example when the next hop is unreachable). The failure detail shows what the best path actually carries.
- **Local preference** is the effective value: a path without a LOCAL_PREF attribute (eBGP-learned or local) gets the device's default (FRR and SONiC: `bgp default local-preference`; SR Linux: the neighbor's `local-preference`; Arista EOS reports it directly). The exception is a locally originated path on Arista EOS, which reports no local preference; asserting `local_pref` on it fails with "not set".
- **Next hop** is the address the device reports. For an IPv6 path FRR may list only the link-local next hop.
- `present: false`, and any attribute key (`communities`, `without_communities`, `as_path`, `as_path_regex`, `local_pref`, `med`, `next_hop`), make it a post-convergence check. The best path can change when a slower session comes up, so an attribute check could pass on a temporary best path before the real one arrives; it is judged only after every BGP session on the node is up and the settle delay, and must hold (0.3.1 and later; 0.3.0 judged attribute checks other than `without_communities` on 2 early samples). A `bgp_route` with no attribute keys (the best path exists) is a positive check.

```yaml
- type: bgp_route         # customer routes are tagged and preferred
  node: r1
  prefix: 192.168.20.0/24
  communities: ["65000:100", no-export]
  local_pref: 200
  as_path: "65020"

- type: bgp_route         # the internal tag must never reach the peer
  node: peer1
  prefix: 192.168.20.0/24
  without_communities: ["65000:666"]
```

### ping

Reachability from a node.

| Key | Required | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `target` | yes | | Destination IP address |
| `source` | no | | Source IP address (passed as `ping -I`) |
| `expect` | no | `success` | `success` or `failure` |
| `count` | no | `3` | Packets to send. An integer from 1 to 1000. |
| `min_replies` | no | `count - 1`, at least 1 | Replies needed for `expect: success`: an integer from 1 to `count`. One lost packet is tolerated by default (first-packet ARP). Not allowed with `expect: failure` |
| `vrf` | no | `default` | Runs in the VRF (`ip vrf exec` on FRR) or network-instance namespace (`srbase-<name>` on SR Linux) |

- `expect: failure` passes only with 0 replies, and is a post-convergence check.
- `expect: failure` also passes when ping reports the destination unreachable without sending anything: "Network unreachable" (or "Network is unreachable"), "No route to host" or "Destination unreachable" (0.3.1 and later). With no route at all, ping prints one of these and no statistics.
- If ping did not run at all for any other reason (bad source address, missing VRF), the check fails with an error. It never counts as a successful "failure".

```yaml
- type: ping
  node: r1
  source: 192.168.1.1
  target: 192.168.3.1
```

## Failure scenarios

`scenarios:` runs extra checks while something is wrong, then puts it right. Use it to prove the network survives a failure, for example that traffic reroutes when an uplink dies, or that your max-prefix limit and import filters hold when a neighbor misbehaves.

```yaml
scenarios:
  - name: r1-r2 link fails
    link_down: {node: r1, interface: eth1}   # or a list of links
    checks:
      - {type: route, node: r1, prefix: 192.168.2.0/24, protocol: bgp}   # rerouted via r3
      - {type: ping, node: r1, source: 192.168.1.1, target: 192.168.2.1}
      - {type: bgp_session, node: r1, neighbor: 10.0.12.2, state: down}

  - node_isolated: r2          # all of r2's lab links down
    checks:
      - {type: route, node: r1, prefix: 192.168.2.0/24, present: false}

  - name: customer floods us
    inject_routes: {node: ce1, count: 200, from: 10.100.16.0/24}   # ce1 announces 200 extra /24s
    checks:
      - {type: bgp_prefixes, node: up1, neighbor: 10.0.2.1, max: 51}   # the max-prefix limit holds

  - name: peer announces what it does not own
    inject_routes: {node: peer1, prefixes: [10.100.0.0/25, 8.8.8.0/24], as_path: [65400]}
    checks:
      - {type: bgp_prefixes, node: pe2, neighbor: 10.0.4.2, max: 1}   # the import filter holds
      - {type: route, node: ce1, prefix: 10.100.0.0/25, protocol: bgp, present: false}
```

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `name` | Label shown before each check (default: generated from the faults) |
| `link_down` | `{node, interface}` or a list of them; no other keys. Interface names as seen inside the node (for example `eth1` on FRR): a Linux interface name of at most 15 letters, digits and `. _ @ -` (checked from 0.3.1). SR Linux links can't be failed yet; fail the FRR or Linux side instead |
| `node_isolated` | A node name, `{node}`, or a list of them: every lab link of that node goes down |
| `inject_routes` | `{node, prefixes}` or `{node, count}` (or a list of them): the node announces extra routes. 0.3.1 and later. See below |
| `checks` | Same check types and keys as the top level. See [scenario timing](#scenario-timing) |

A scenario needs at least one fault and at least one check, and accepts no other keys. Scenarios run after the main checks, one at a time.
