That way the agent can pass the path its own file tools use. Before this, an agent on Windows had to translate paths itself, and in the [agent evaluation](#measured-ten-tickets-worked-unattended) a smaller model did not.

`dry_run` takes 30 seconds to several minutes. Start Claude Code with a longer tool timeout, in milliseconds, so it does not give up first:

```bash
MCP_TOOL_TIMEOUT=600000 claude
```

See [MCP tool calls time out](troubleshooting.md#mcp-tool-calls-time-out-in-the-client).

### Other MCP clients

Configure a stdio server with command `netdryrun` and argument `mcp`. Most clients take JSON like this (this is the `.mcp.json` Claude Code wrote above, with the Linux command):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "netdryrun": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "netdryrun",
      "args": ["mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

Without installing, use `"command": "uvx", "args": ["netdryrun", "mcp"]`. On Windows, use the `wsl.exe` command and arguments shown above. Set the client's tool-call timeout to at least 5 minutes.

## Workflow

1. The agent writes its proposed change into the lab's configs (in a lab folder with a containerlab topology and a `netdryrun.yml`).
2. It calls `dry_run` on that folder.
3. It applies the change elsewhere only if `status` is `passed`.

## Demo: a ticket, a tempting change, a verdict


[`examples/agent-demo`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples/agent-demo): the customer's new block must reach the upstream and the peer. The tempting change, removing the prefix-list filters, passes every ticket check, session check and ping, but leaks upstream routes and the upstream's default route to the peer, and accepts a prefix the customer doesn't own. The network team's leak guards fail, so the verdict is `DO NOT APPLY THIS CHANGE`. The proper fix, two prefix-list lines, passes the same checks. The checks never change; only the config does. Both attempts are a scripted replay (hand-written diffs, not output from a real agent); `demo.sh` runs them, and CI runs it on pushes to `main` and on pull requests. In a [real run](#a-real-agent-run), a fresh Claude Code agent with only the ticket, the lab and these MCP tools made the correct two-line change on the first try and proposed it with a `passed` verdict.

## Give the agent a ticket (the TICKET.md pattern)

An agent does better with a written task and explicit rules than with a chat message. Put a `TICKET.md` in the lab folder, next to `topology.clab.yml`, `configs/` and `netdryrun.yml`. [`examples/agent-demo/TICKET.md`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/examples/agent-demo/TICKET.md) is a complete example. A ticket says:

- **The goal, in network terms.** "The customer's new block 10.101.0.0/24 must reach the upstream and the peer." Name the routers, ASes and prefixes.
- **What the agent may change.** "Change only `configs/edge1.conf`." A small allowed surface makes the change easy to review.
- **What it must not change.** "Don't edit `netdryrun.yml`." The checks belong to the network team. An agent that may edit the checks can make any change pass.
- **The gate.** "Before proposing the change, run Netdryrun on this folder (`netdryrun run <folder>`, or the `dry_run` MCP tool) and include the verdict. Propose it only if the status is `passed`."

Then the prompt can stay short. The real run below used: "Work the ticket in TICKET.md in the current folder, following its rules", plus the path the MCP tools use for the folder and a request for the diff and the verdict at the end. Nothing about the solution.

More guidance for the prompt or the agent's instructions file:

- Ask for the verdict and the names of any failed checks in the final answer, so a human can review the evidence instead of the agent's reasoning.
- Tell it what to do on a failure: read `detail` for each failed check, fix the config, run again. Never weaken or delete a check; if it thinks a check is wrong, it should say so and stop.
- Don't show it the answer. In `examples/agent-demo`, the README, `changes/` and `demo.sh` contain the solution, so the real run could only see `TICKET.md`, `netdryrun.yml`, `topology.clab.yml` and `configs/`.
- A pass covers only the checks that exist. Give the agent the network team's standing guards (leak checks, `present: false` routes), not only the ticket's acceptance checks.

The repository's [`AGENTS.md`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/AGENTS.md) has the same rules written for agents.

## A real agent run

[`AGENT-RUN.md`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/examples/agent-demo/AGENT-RUN.md) records one real run on `examples/agent-demo`, not the scripted replay:

- **Agent:** Claude Code 2.1.116 in headless mode (`claude -p`). It could read and edit files and call the Netdryrun MCP tools. No shell, no web access, so its only way to test was Netdryrun.
- **What it did:** read the ticket, the router config and `netdryrun.yml`; added the new block to the two prefix lists in `configs/edge1.conf`; called `dry_run`; got `status: passed`, 14 of 14 checks, verdict `SAFE TO PROCEED`; proposed the two-line change with the verdict. 7 turns, 69 seconds.
- **Checked afterwards:** it changed only `configs/edge1.conf`, and a fresh `netdryrun run` on its folder gave `PASSED: 14 passed, 0 failed`.

The agent did not make the tempting leaky change, so this run did not show Netdryrun catching a mistake (`demo.sh` shows that). It shows the workflow end to end: the agent found the tool, ran the network team's checks through MCP, and its proposal came with a verdict from a real lab. It is one run of one model on one ticket.

## Measured: ten tickets worked unattended

One good run is an anecdote, so on 2026-10-27 we measured. [`examples/agent-eval`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples/agent-eval) has ten tickets on the two FRR example labs: changes to make, colleagues' changes to review (some fine, some leaking routes or setting the wrong attribute while sessions and pings stay up), a request that is itself a route leak, and one broken lab. Each has a hidden grader. The expected answers were [pre-registered](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/examples/agent-eval/PREREGISTRATION.md) before anything ran. A fresh headless Claude Code agent worked each ticket alone, with only `AGENTS.md`, this page and the MCP tools: no shell, no project memory, no human.

| Agent (Claude Code 2.1.116) | Netdryrun | Solved | Misses |
|---|---|---|---|
| `claude-opus-4-7`, two runs | 0.3.0 | 10 / 10, 10 / 10 | none |
| `claude-haiku-4-5`, one run (not pre-registered: the prediction covered only the default model) | 0.3.0 | 3 / 10 | 5 ended on a Windows/WSL path mix-up (below); T09, T06 |
| `claude-haiku-4-5`, two runs (not pre-registered) | with the fixes below | 9 / 10 (8 counted strictly, see T07 in RESULTS.md), 8 / 10 | T09 both times; T10 once |

Solved means: finished unattended, the right verdict (safe, harmful or inconclusive), the right decision (apply, don't apply, rerun), no file changed that the ticket forbids, and, for a change it wrote, an independent rerun with extra hidden checks passes.

What failed, and what changed because of it:

- **Paths on Windows.** Claude Code on Windows with the server in WSL is the setup this page documents. The smaller model passed the WSL path (`/mnt/c/...`) to its Windows file tools and was refused, and Netdryrun 0.3.0 refused the Windows path. From 0.3.1 the tools accept both.
- **A pass that covers too little (T09).** A "pure refactor" to `redistribute connected` also announces r1's link subnets. The given checks don't look at that, so Netdryrun says `passed`. The smaller model trusted the pass every time. The larger one caught it by reading the diff, not with Netdryrun. `record_baseline` would have shown it, and no agent used it. `AGENTS.md` now says a "no behavior change" ticket needs a baseline.
- **A broken lab that says `failed` (T10).** With `bgpd` off on every router, the result is `failed`, not `inconclusive`: the inconclusive rule is conservative. From 0.3.1, failed checks that never got usable state carry `"unready": true`. Once, the smaller model turned `bgpd` back on in a file the ticket forbade and said apply.
- **No fix-and-rerun loop.** No agent made a wrong change and then fixed it to a pass: the larger model got every change right first time. So this doesn't measure that loop.
- **A non-deterministic lab.** One wrong-looking change (a bare `network 192.168.0.0/16`) passed 5 of 8 runs. A single `passed` can be luck when the lab itself varies.

The harness set `NETDRYRUN_MCP_ROOT` to the ticket folder, but 0.3.0 ignores that variable, so in the 0.3.0 runs the server was not confined to the folder; the agents had no shell.

Ten small tickets written by the tool's author, two models, at most two runs each: evidence about the docs and the tool surface, not a rate. Full results, transcripts and every miss: [RESULTS.md](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/examples/agent-eval/RESULTS.md).

## Gate agent-made pull requests in CI

An agent's own `dry_run` is a claim. Run the same checks again in CI, where the agent cannot change the result:

```yaml title=".github/workflows/network-dryrun.yml"
name: Network dry run
on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - "network/**"
permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write
jobs:
  dryrun:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: netdryrun/netdryrun@v0.3.1
        with:
          path: network/
          pr-comment: true
```

Then, in the repository settings:

- **Make the job a required status check** on the default branch, so a failed verdict blocks the merge.
- **Protect the checks.** Add a `CODEOWNERS` line such as `network/netdryrun.yml @your-org/network-team` and require code-owner review. A PR that edits the checks then needs a human from the network team, while config-only PRs need only the green check and a normal review.
- **Keep agent PRs away from secrets.** The lab runs as root on the runner. Follow the [Action security notes](github-action.md#security-notes): no secrets in the job, no `pull_request_target`.

The PR comment lists failures first with their evidence, so the reviewer sees what the lab saw. See [GitHub Action](github-action.md) for every input.

## Tools

The server has these tools: `dry_run`, `verify_change`, `run_checks`, `record_baseline`, `validate` and `check_types`.


| Tool | Arguments | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `dry_run` | `path`, `keep_lab` (default `false`) | The primary tool. Deploy the lab, run every check, destroy the lab, return the verdict. Takes about 60–120 s for a small lab; longer with big labs or long timeouts. |
| `run_checks` | `path` | Run the checks against a lab that is already running (no deploy or destroy) |
| `record_baseline` | `topology`, `deploy` (default `true`), `wait_seconds` (default `45`) | Deploy the lab, snapshot its BGP sessions, prefix counts and routes as `netdryrun.yml` text, destroy the lab. Returns the YAML; nothing is written to disk. Like [`netdryrun record`](reference/cli.md#record) |
| `validate` | `path` | Validate `netdryrun.yml` and its topology without starting a lab: node names, drivers and supported keys, as `dry_run` checks them before deploying (0.3.1 and later) |
| `check_types` | | List supported check types and their keys, to help write `netdryrun.yml` |
| `verify_change` | `topology`, `before`, `after`, `intent`, `guards` (optional) | 0.4, FRR only. Boot the topology with the *before* and the *after* configs, diff routing behavior, and fail on every difference the intent doesn't declare. No checks needed. Two lab boots: about 2–4 minutes. See [below](#verify-a-change-against-the-tickets-intent) |

The server also exposes the last full JSON report as a resource, `netdryrun://report/{path}`.

From 0.3.2, every tool description carries the same rules, so an agent that reads only one tool still gets them: use it before proposing or applying a routing or policy change; ping is not a test; a dry run takes about 60–120 s; it needs Linux or WSL2, Docker and containerlab with root-equivalent rights and won't run on macOS or in sandboxes without Docker-in-Docker; inconclusive means stop, don't retry more than once; never invent or weaken checks, and call `record_baseline` if no checks exist (from 0.4: or `verify_change` with the intent the ticket states).

## Verify a change against the ticket's intent

New in 0.4, FRR only. Checks cover what someone thought of; an agent asked to make a change tends to check only what it meant to change, and so misses what it broke. `verify_change` inverts that: the agent passes the intent, and **every other difference in the network's behavior fails**. When a repository has no `netdryrun.yml` and the ticket says what the change should do, prefer `verify_change` over writing checks.

```json
{"topology": "C:\\net\\lab\\topology.clab.yml", "before": "main", "after": "C:\\net\\lab-after",
 "intent": "intent:\n  - prefix: 10.101.0.0/24\n    appears_on: [edge1, up1, peer1]\n"}
```

- `before` and `after` are each a git ref or a directory holding the lab's tree, as for [`netdryrun verify`](reference/verify.md). The topology file must be the same on both sides.
- `intent` is the [intent](reference/verify.md#the-intent-file) as YAML or JSON text, or the path of an intent file. **It comes from the ticket or the operator**: never write it from the diff, and never widen it (or add `allow_anywhere`) to make a change pass. The result records `intent_source: "mcp"`.
- `guards` is an optional `netdryrun.yml` run on the *after* lab. With a git ref as `before`, the `netdryrun.yml` next to the topology in that ref runs by default, so the base branch's leak guards fail a change even when the intent declares the leak.

The `verdict` is `INTENT MATCHED`, `UNDECLARED CHANGES: DO NOT APPLY` or `INCONCLUSIVE`, plus `NO BEHAVIOR CHANGE` (nothing changed and nothing was declared), `INCONCLUSIVE: UNHEALTHY BASELINE` and `ERROR: NO VERDICT`. It never says `SAFE TO PROCEED`: explained is not the same as safe, so show the echoed `intent` to the human with the verdict. On `UNDECLARED CHANGES`, `undeclared` lists each difference nobody declared (up to 50; `undeclared_total` counts them) with one read-only `next_diagnostic` command, and `not_happened` the declarations that didn't happen. Fix the change, not the intent. The full report, both snapshots included, is in `evidence_file`. The result format is `$defs/verify_result` in [`mcp-result-v1.json`](https://netdryrun.com/schemas/mcp-result-v1.json).

## Result and verdict

`dry_run` and `run_checks` return JSON like this:

```json
{
  "schema": "netdryrun.mcp-result/v1",
  "status": "failed",
  "passed": 5,
  "failed": 1,
  "error": null,
  "inconclusive_reason": null,
  "lab": "ndr-frr-broken",
  "checks": [
    {"name": "r1: route 0.0.0.0/0 via bgp is absent", "passed": false,
     "detail": "unexpectedly present via bgp (not selected)"}
  ],
  "failures": [
    {"check": "r1: route 0.0.0.0/0 via bgp is absent", "node": "r1",
     "reason": "unexpectedly present via bgp (not selected)",
     "evidence": {"cmd": "vtysh -c show ip route 0.0.0.0/0 json", "rc": 0,
                  "excerpt": "{ \"0.0.0.0/0\":[ { \"prefix\":\"0.0.0.0/0\", \"prefixLen\":0, \"protocol\":\"bgp\", ..."},
     "next_diagnostic": "docker exec clab-ndr-frr-broken-r1 vtysh -c 'show ip route 0.0.0.0/0'"}
  ],
  "evidence_file": "/path/to/lab/netdryrun-report.json",
  "verdict": "DO NOT APPLY THIS CHANGE"
}
```

(`checks` is shortened here; the real result lists every check.)

From 0.3.2, `failures` lists each failed check with:

- `check` and `node`: the check name and the node it reads;
- `reason`: the one-line reason it failed;
- `evidence`: a short excerpt of the raw evidence (the first command of the final sample that failed, else the last command run), flattened to one line and capped at 200 characters; `null` if no command ran;
- `next_diagnostic`: one read-only command that shows the state the check looked at, in that node's own CLI (`vtysh` on FRR and SONiC, `Cli` on EOS, `sr_cli` on SR Linux); `null` if the node's driver or container is unknown. It needs the lab running: `dry_run` destroys the lab, so rerun it with `keep_lab: true`, run the command, then destroy the lab with `containerlab destroy -t <topology>`.

The format is a published JSON Schema, [`mcp-result-v1.json`](https://netdryrun.com/schemas/mcp-result-v1.json), which also covers the results of `validate`, `check_types` and `record_baseline` errors. Within v1, fields are only added, never removed or renamed. The test suite validates the results of real lab runs against it.

From 0.3.1, a failed check also has `"unready": true` when every sample of it failed for lack of state: the command failed on the device, its output could not be read, or BGP had no neighbors at all. That points at the lab as much as at the change. The [inconclusive rule](reference/cli.md#when-a-run-is-inconclusive) is conservative, so a lab where a daemon never started can still come back `failed` when other nodes' route and ping checks read cleanly. If the `unready` failures and details such as `bgpd is not running` sit on nodes the change doesn't explain, report the lab problem; don't rewrite the change, and don't apply it.

`verdict` is a separate field with one of three values. They are frozen: within v1 of the result schema they never change, so an agent can match on them exactly.

- `SAFE TO PROCEED` when `status` is `passed`. It means every check in the file passed in the lab, and nothing more: a change that breaks something no check looks at gets it too (ticket T09 above). For a change that must not change behavior, record a baseline first
- `DO NOT APPLY THIS CHANGE` for `failed` or `error`, including config errors
- `INCONCLUSIVE: the lab did not reach a testable state; this says nothing about your change. Do not apply it until a run passes.` when `status` is `inconclusive`: the lab never came up far enough for the checks to mean anything ([rules](reference/cli.md#when-a-run-is-inconclusive)). `inconclusive_reason` says what was seen. Rerun it, perhaps with a longer `timeout`; don't rewrite the change because of it.

Tell the agent what to do with each verdict: propose the change only on `SAFE TO PROCEED`; on `DO NOT APPLY THIS CHANGE`, read the failed checks, fix the config and run again; on `INCONCLUSIVE`, stop: rerun at most once, and if it stays inconclusive, report that the lab does not come up instead of changing the config. [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md#inconclusive-the-lab-never-came-up) shows a real inconclusive run.

The full evidence is written to `netdryrun-report.json` next to `netdryrun.yml`. Its format, `netdryrun.report/v1`, is defined by a JSON Schema: [`report-v1.json`](https://netdryrun.com/schemas/report-v1.json), also published as an open spec any tool can emit: [Network Change Verdict v1](spec/verdict-v1.md). The test suite validates reports from real lab runs against it.

## The agent skill

[`skills/netdryrun/SKILL.md`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/skills/netdryrun/SKILL.md) (from 0.3.2) gives a coding agent the rules in one file: before applying a routing change, dry-run it; paste the verdict; stop on inconclusive; never write or weaken checks to make a change pass; use `record_baseline` when there are no checks. Install it from the repository's git URL:

```bash
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun /tmp/netdryrun
mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills && cp -r /tmp/netdryrun/skills/netdryrun ~/.claude/skills/   # Claude Code, every project
```

To give it to everyone working in one repository, copy the folder to `.claude/skills/netdryrun/` there and commit it. Other clients that read Agent Skills (a folder with a `SKILL.md`) take the same folder.

## Paste this into your network repository's AGENTS.md

Coding agents read `AGENTS.md` at the root of a repository. Put these lines in the one for your network configs, so every agent that works there dry-runs its changes:

```markdown
Before proposing or applying any routing or policy change in this repository, dry-run it: `netdryrun run <lab>` or the `dry_run` MCP tool. Propose the change only if the verdict is SAFE TO PROCEED. Ping is not a test. Never edit `netdryrun.yml` to make a change pass.
```

Replace `<lab>` with the folder that holds your `netdryrun.yml`. Protect that file with a `CODEOWNERS` line, as in [the CI gate above](#gate-agent-made-pull-requests-in-ci), so the checks stay with the network team.

## Safety model

- **It never touches production.** The server has no tool that pushes config anywhere. It only builds and tests labs.
- **No full device output in tool results.** Tool results contain normalized check results (name, pass/fail, a short detail), not full command output; that goes to the JSON report file. A detail or an error can still quote a fragment of lab text, such as a BGP state name or the last line of a failed command, so from 0.3.1 each is flattened to one line and capped at 300 characters (1,000 for errors). From 0.3.2 a failed check also carries an evidence excerpt, flattened the same way and capped at 200 characters. The `status` and `verdict` are computed from pass/fail only, never from that text: an agent should act on them and treat `detail`, `reason`, `error` and excerpts as data.
- **Labs are code.** containerlab runs privileged containers. Only point the server at topologies you trust, on a machine you would let run Docker. The tools take any path the agent passes, and a `netdryrun.yml` can point at a topology in another folder. To keep an agent to one folder (Netdryrun 0.3.1 and later; 0.3.0 ignores the variable without a warning), set `NETDRYRUN_MCP_ROOT` in the server's environment (several folders separated by `:`, or `;` on Windows): every `netdryrun.yml`, the lab it points to and every topology must then resolve inside it, or the tool refuses. This stops an agent from being steered to a lab elsewhere; it does not make an untrusted lab inside the folder safe, since a topology can still mount host paths.

A pass is evidence from a lab, not a guarantee about production. See [what a lab cannot prove](trust.md#what-a-lab-cannot-prove).


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/troubleshooting/

# Troubleshooting

Each error below was reproduced on purpose on WSL2 (Ubuntu 22.04) with containerlab 0.81.1 and Netdryrun™ 0.3.1, and the output is copied from those runs. The labs are copies of the [tutorial](tutorial.md)'s `my-lab` (lab name `ndr-my-lab`) and of the bundled examples, renamed `ndr-docs-*`. Where an entry shows what an older version did, it says which version.

Exit code `2` means the run has no verdict (a config error, a lab error, a fault that did not take effect, or an internal error; `--debug` shows the traceback of an internal error). Exit code `1` means a check failed. See [exit codes](reference/cli.md#exit-codes).

## Unknown key ... did you mean

```text
$ netdryrun validate my-lab
config error: checks[11]: unknown keys ['presnt'] for type route; did you mean 'present'?; allowed: active, hold, name, node, prefix, present, protocol, timeout, type, vrf
```

Exit code `2`. From 0.3.1, a key Netdryrun doesn't know is an error at every level of the file (top level, `nodes`, checks, scenarios and their faults), not only inside checks. Before 0.3.1, a misspelled key at the top level, under `nodes` or inside a fault was ignored: a whole block of checks under `chekcs:` never ran, and nothing said so. 0.3.1 says `unknown top-level keys ['chekcs']; did you mean 'checks'?; allowed: checks, lab, nodes, scenarios, timeout`. Fix the spelling the message suggests; `allowed:` lists every key that fits there. The same goes for values from a fixed list (`afi`, `protocol`, `state`, `expect`, `driver`), and a key written twice in the same mapping is an error too (`not valid YAML at line 55, column 3: duplicate key 'present' (first defined on line 54)`). Run `netdryrun validate` after upgrading: a file that 0.3.0 accepted can fail here, and every such failure was a check that didn't test what it said.

## containerlab is not installed

```text
$ netdryrun run my-lab
Netdryrun 0.3.1: 14 checks from my-lab/netdryrun.yml
ERROR: 'containerlab' not found on PATH
```

Exit code `2`. Netdryrun drives the `containerlab` CLI and needs it on `PATH`. Install it ([containerlab.dev/install](https://containerlab.dev/install/)) and check with `containerlab version`. The same error names `docker` if Docker is missing. Nothing was deployed, so nothing is destroyed.

## Docker or containerlab permission denied

Without the `docker` group (here, with every supplementary group dropped), Netdryrun stops before deploying anything, because its first step is to ask Docker whether a lab with the same name is already running:

```text
$ netdryrun run my-lab
Netdryrun 0.3.1: 14 checks from my-lab/netdryrun.yml
ERROR: could not list Docker containers: permission denied while trying to connect to the docker API at unix:///var/run/docker.sock
```

Exit code `2`. `docker ps` fails the same way:

```text
$ docker ps
permission denied while trying to connect to the docker API at unix:///var/run/docker.sock
```

A user in `docker` but not in `clab_admins` gets past that, and then containerlab refuses the deploy. Its message, from a run with Netdryrun 0.2.0 as a user `ndrtest`:

```text
ERROR: containerlab deploy failed:

   ERROR

  User 'ndrtest' is not part of containerlab admin group 'clab_admins', which is required to execute this command.
  To add yourself to this group, run the following command:
      $ sudo usermod -aG clab_admins ndrtest.
```

Fix: add your user to both groups, then start a new login session so the groups apply.

```bash
sudo usermod -aG docker,clab_admins "$USER"
```

On WSL, close the terminal and run `wsl --shutdown` from Windows, then open it again. Check with `id`: both groups must be listed.

```text
$ id
uid=1001(ndrtest) gid=1001(ndrtest) groups=1001(ndrtest),998(clab_admins),999(docker)
```

After this, the same user deployed and ran the lab. Running Netdryrun with `sudo` also works, but then the reports are owned by root.

## A check names a node that is not in the topology

A typo (`r9` instead of `r1`) is caught before anything is deployed:

```text
$ netdryrun run unk
Netdryrun 0.3.1: 14 checks from unk/netdryrun.yml
ERROR: unknown node(s) r9; the topology has r1, r2, r3
```

From 0.3.1, `netdryrun validate` reads the topology too and catches it without starting anything (`lab error: unknown node(s) r9; ...`). Before 0.3.1, `validate` checked only the file itself and printed `OK` for this typo.

Exit code `2`, and nothing is deployed or destroyed: from 0.3.1, a lab you kept running with `--keep` survives a typo like this (0.3.0 and earlier destroyed it). Use the node names from the topology's `nodes:` section (`r1`), not the container names (`clab-ndr-my-lab-r1`).

## The lab never converges (timeout)

A positive check waits up to `timeout` seconds (default 120) for the network to converge, then fails. Here r1 has the wrong `remote-as` for r2 and `timeout` is 30:

```text
$ netdryrun run slow
Netdryrun 0.3.1: 14 checks from slow/netdryrun.yml
Deploying lab ndr-docs-slow (3 nodes); this usually takes 30-90 s, longer the first time images are pulled...
  [PASS] r1: BGP session to 10.0.13.2 is established -- state is established (13.3s)
  ...
  [FAIL] r1: BGP session to 10.0.12.2 is established -- state is idle (30.0s)
  [FAIL] r2: BGP session to 10.0.12.1 is established -- state is idle (30.0s)
Convergence checks done; settling 10s before post-convergence checks...
  [FAIL] r1: prefixes from 10.0.12.2 >= 2 and <= 10 -- not evaluated: BGP session(s) on r1 not established: 10.0.12.2 (idle) after waiting 30s. A post-convergence check only means something once every BGP session on its node is up (a leak can arrive over any of them). If a session is down on purpose, add a bgp_session check with state: down for it (30.0s)
  ...
Destroying lab...
FAILED: 8 passed, 6 failed (14 checks)
```

A check that fails at exactly its timeout (`30.0s` here) never reached the expected state. Two causes:

- **The change really breaks something.** The `detail` says what the router reported (`state is idle`). This is the test working.
- **The lab is slow to boot.** SR Linux, SONiC and cEOS take longer than FRR. Raise `timeout` at the top of `netdryrun.yml`, or on one check. `examples/srl-frr` uses 120.

To see why, keep the lab and look inside:

```text
$ netdryrun run slow --keep-on-failure
...
Lab ndr-docs-slow left running for debugging; destroy with: containerlab destroy -t /home/ndr/work/docs031/ts/slow/topology.clab.yml --cleanup
FAILED: 8 passed, 6 failed (14 checks)
$ docker exec clab-ndr-docs-slow-r1 vtysh -c "show bgp summary"
...
Neighbor        V         AS   MsgRcvd   MsgSent   TblVer  InQ OutQ  Up/Down State/PfxRcd   PfxSnt Desc
10.0.12.2       4      65099         6        12        0    0    0    never         Idle        0 N/A
r3(10.0.13.2)   4      65003        34        40        4    0    0 00:01:06            3        4 FRRouting/10.4.1_git
```

r1 expects AS 65099 at 10.0.12.2, but r2 is AS 65002. Destroy the lab with the command Netdryrun printed.

The routes still arrive over the r1-r3 session, so the route and ping checks pass. r1's four post-convergence checks (the two prefix counts with `max`, and the two routes that must be absent) report `not evaluated`, because one of r1's sessions is down; see the next entry.

## Not evaluated (a session on the node never came up)

```text
  [FAIL] r1: prefixes from 10.0.12.2 >= 2 and <= 10 -- not evaluated: BGP session(s) on r1 not established: 10.0.12.2 (idle) after waiting 30s. A post-convergence check only means something once every BGP session on its node is up (a leak can arrive over any of them). If a session is down on purpose, add a bgp_session check with state: down for it
```

Exit code `1`. From 0.3.1, a post-convergence check (a route that must be absent, a ping that must fail, a prefix count with `max` or `exact`, a `bgp_route` attribute) starts only once every configured BGP neighbor on its node is up with stable prefix counts. A leak can arrive over any session, so a check that passed while one was still down would prove nothing. Netdryrun waits up to the largest `timeout` of the node's post-convergence checks; if a session is still down then, those checks fail as `not evaluated` and name the session.

Fix: if the session should be up, it's a finding: look at it as in [the lab never converges](#the-lab-never-converges-timeout), or raise `timeout` for a slow NOS. If it is down on purpose (a shut neighbor, a peer that isn't in the lab), add a check that says so, and the wait leaves it out:

```yaml
- type: bgp_session
  node: r1
  neighbor: 10.0.12.2
  state: down
```

## A node without BGP waits a whole timeout

```text
warning: h1 reported no BGP neighbors for 30s; the check was evaluated without BGP convergence
```

From 0.3.1, a node that answers with no BGP neighbors at all is treated as not converged yet, because that is also what a router answers before its BGP config is applied. Its post-convergence checks (a ping that must fail, for example) wait up to their `timeout`, then run with this warning in their result; the verdict is unchanged. On a node that really doesn't run BGP, lower the `timeout` of those checks to shorten the wait. If the node should have BGP neighbors, its BGP config was never applied: check its startup config or `setup` commands.

## The fault did not take effect

```text
ERROR: scenario 'r1-r2 link fails': the fault did not take effect within 30s: BGP session(s) over the downed links still established (r2 -> 10.0.12.1). Netdryrun won't judge the scenario's checks on the state from before the fault. Without BFD, BGP can take its hold time (up to 180 s) to notice a failure: raise the checks' timeout, or lower the hold timers in the lab
```

Exit code `2`. From 0.3.1, after taking links down a scenario waits until every BGP session that ran over them is down on both ends, so its checks are never judged on the state from before the failure. The wait is capped at the largest `timeout` of the scenario's checks. Here the far end, r2, still had the session up when the time ran out: without BFD, a router notices a dead link only when its BGP hold timer expires (180 s on FRR by default).

Fix: give the scenario's checks a `timeout` above the hold time (for example `timeout: 200` on them, or at the top of the file), lower the hold timers in the lab configs (`timers bgp 3 9` on FRR), or enable BFD. The links are restored and the lab destroyed as usual. See [scenario timing](reference/config.md#scenario-timing).

## Could not read BGP state to find the sessions over the links

```text
ERROR: could not read BGP state on r2 to find the BGP sessions over the links the scenario takes down: `vtysh -c show bgp neighbors json` failed on r2 (rc=1): bgpd is not running. Netdryrun won't judge the scenario without knowing when the fault took effect
```

Reproduced with a copy of `examples/frr-bgp` whose r2 starts without `bgpd`: the main checks on r1 run (the session to r2 fails), then the `r1-r2 link fails` scenario stops here.

Exit code `2`. From 0.3.1, before a scenario takes links down, Netdryrun reads the BGP state of the nodes on both ends of each link (and the addresses of the downed interfaces) to know which sessions the fault must bring down. If that state can't be read, it can't tell when the fault took effect, so it stops before changing anything instead of judging the scenario on the settle delay alone (0.3.0 read it as "no sessions"). Usually the node's routing daemon is still starting or has crashed: check the node (`docker exec <container> vtysh -c "show bgp summary"`), raise the main checks' `timeout` so the lab is fully up before the scenarios start, and rerun. A node no driver can read (a Linux host) and a VRF the node doesn't have count as "no sessions", as before.

## SR Linux fails on a Windows drive (/mnt/c)

On WSL, files under `/mnt/c` are on the Windows filesystem, which has no Linux permissions. If containerlab's lab directory is there, SR Linux cannot save its config. Running containerlab directly in such a folder (a copy of `examples/srl-frr`):

```text
$ containerlab deploy -t topology.clab.yml
09:54:58 INFO Creating lab directory path=/mnt/c/Users/.../d031_srlmnt/clab-ndr-docs-srlmnt
09:54:58 INFO unable to adjust Labdir file ACLs: operation not supported
...
09:55:15 ERRO node "srl1" post-deploy: command execution error:Error in /system:
    Setting permissions for file '/etc/opt/srlinux/config.tmp' failed with error_code = 1 [Operation not permitted]
Error: Commit failed
```

containerlab exits with an error, but the SR Linux container keeps running without its startup config until you destroy the lab. If you point Netdryrun's lab directory there yourself (`CLAB_LABDIR_BASE` under `/mnt/`), the run stops at the deploy, with exit code `2`:

```text
$ CLAB_LABDIR_BASE=$PWD netdryrun run .
Netdryrun 0.3.1: 7 checks from netdryrun.yml
Deploying lab ndr-docs-srlmnt (2 nodes); this usually takes 30-90 s, longer the first time images are pulled...
Destroying lab...
ERROR: containerlab deploy failed:
...
09:55:36 ERRO node "srl1" post-deploy: command execution error:Error in /system:
    Setting permissions for file '/etc/opt/srlinux/config.tmp' failed with error_code = 1 [Operation not permitted]
Error: Commit failed
```

Without that, Netdryrun avoids this. When the topology is under `/mnt/`, it puts containerlab's lab directory in `~/.cache/netdryrun/labs` (unless you set `CLAB_LABDIR_BASE` yourself). The same folder with `netdryrun run .`:

```text
$ netdryrun run .
Netdryrun 0.3.1: 7 checks from netdryrun.yml
Deploying lab ndr-docs-srlmnt (2 nodes); this usually takes 30-90 s, longer the first time images are pulled...
  [PASS] srl1: BGP session to 10.0.100.2 is established -- state is established (32.8s)
  ...
PASSED: 7 passed, 0 failed (7 checks)
```

If you deploy with containerlab yourself (for example for `netdryrun check`), either keep the lab on the Linux filesystem (`~/...`) or set `CLAB_LABDIR_BASE` to a Linux path. Keeping labs on the Linux filesystem is also faster.

## The cEOS image is missing

Arista does not allow cEOS to be redistributed, so you import it yourself. If the image named in the topology is not in Docker, Docker tries to pull it from Docker Hub and fails:

```text
$ netdryrun run ceos
Netdryrun 0.3.1: 8 checks from ceos/netdryrun.yml
Deploying lab ndr-docs-ceos (2 nodes); this usually takes 30-90 s, longer the first time images are pulled...
Destroying lab...
ERROR: containerlab deploy failed:
09:38:28 INFO Containerlab started version=0.81.1
09:38:28 INFO Parsing & checking topology file=topology.clab.yml
09:38:28 INFO Removing directory path=/home/ndr/work/docs031/ts/ceos/clab-ndr-docs-ceos
09:38:28 INFO Creating docker network name=clab IPv4 subnet=172.20.20.0/24 IPv6 subnet=3fff:172:20:20::/64 MTU=0
09:38:28 INFO Pulling image image=docker.io/library/ceos:4.34.1F
09:38:30 ERRO Failed to pull image image=docker.io/library/ceos:4.34.1F err="Error response from daemon: pull access denied for ceos, repository does not exist or may require 'docker login'"
...
```

Exit code `2`. This is a copy of `examples/arista-frr` with the image changed to a tag that isn't in Docker.

Fix: download cEOS-lab from arista.com (free account) and import it with the exact name and tag the topology uses: `docker import cEOS-lab-<version>.tar ceos:<version>`, as the comment in `examples/arista-frr/topology.clab.yml` says. Then check that Docker has it:

```text
$ docker images ceos
IMAGE          ID             DISK USAGE   CONTENT SIZE   EXTRA
ceos:4.36.3M   94cc1e5462fe       3.55GB          976MB
```

`examples/arista-frr` expects `ceos:4.36.3M`. Either import with that tag or change `image:` in the topology to match yours.

## A lab named X is already running

```text
$ netdryrun run other-lab
Netdryrun 0.3.1: 14 checks from other-lab/netdryrun.yml
ERROR: a lab named 'ndr-my-lab' is already running (3 container(s), e.g. clab-ndr-my-lab-r1): another Netdryrun run, or a lab deployed by hand or kept with --keep. Netdryrun won't redeploy or destroy it. Wait for the other run to finish, or remove the lab with: containerlab destroy -t /home/ndr/work/docs031/ts/other-lab/topology.clab.yml --cleanup
```

Here `my-lab` was left running with `--keep`, then `other-lab`, a copy with the same `name:`, was run.

Exit code `2`, before anything is deployed. containerlab lab names are global on a machine: containers are named `clab-<lab>-<node>`. From 0.3.1, `netdryrun run` refuses to deploy a lab whose name is already in use, because redeploying would reconfigure the other lab's containers, and destroying it afterwards would remove them from under whoever is using it. Two runs of the same lab started at the same moment on one host get `another Netdryrun run is already using lab 'ndr-my-lab' on this host; wait for it to finish (two runs of the same lab would collide)` instead, and the first run carries on.

Fix: wait for the other run, destroy the old lab with the command in the message (for a lab you kept with `--keep` or `--keep-on-failure`), or give every lab a unique `name:`. On a shared CI runner or machine, put something unique in the name (for example the branch). `netdryrun check` doesn't deploy, so it still runs against the running lab.

Before 0.3.1, Netdryrun deployed with `containerlab deploy --reconfigure` regardless, so a second lab with the same `name:` **replaced** the first one, even from a different folder. Here, on 0.2.0, `my-lab` was left running with `--keep`, then a copy of it in `other-lab` (same `name: my-lab`) was run:

```text
$ netdryrun run other-lab
Netdryrun 0.2.0: 14 checks from other-lab/netdryrun.yml
Deploying lab my-lab (3 nodes)...
...
Destroying lab...
```

The first lab is gone:

```text
$ netdryrun check my-lab
Netdryrun 0.2.0: 14 checks from my-lab/netdryrun.yml
ERROR: lab containers not running: clab-my-lab-r1, clab-my-lab-r2, clab-my-lab-r3
```

Before you run, check what is up with `docker ps` or `containerlab inspect --all`.

## A host port is already in use

If a topology publishes ports on the host (`ports:` on a node), two containers cannot use the same host port, whether they are in two labs or in one. Here r1 and r2 of the same lab both publish `18179:179`:

```text
$ netdryrun run p2
Netdryrun 0.3.1: 14 checks from p2/netdryrun.yml
Deploying lab ndr-docs-p2 (3 nodes); this usually takes 30-90 s, longer the first time images are pulled...
Destroying lab...
ERROR: containerlab deploy failed:
...
09:53:26 ERRO node "r2" deploy: Error response from daemon: failed to set up container networking: driver failed programming external connectivity on endpoint clab-ndr-docs-p2-r2 (cd360913...): Bind for 0.0.0.0:18179 failed: port is already allocated
```

Exit code `2`.

Fix: Netdryrun does not need published ports; it runs every command with `docker exec`. Remove `ports:` from the topology, or use different host ports per lab. `docker ps` shows which container holds the port.

## link_down on an SR Linux node

Failure scenarios take links down with `ip link` inside the node, which works on FRR, SONiC and cEOS but not yet on SR Linux. From 0.3.1, `netdryrun validate` refuses the file (exit code `2`). `run` finds out only when the scenario starts, after the main checks:

```text
$ netdryrun validate srl-ld
lab error: failure scenarios on SR Linux nodes (srl1) are not supported yet; take the link down on the FRR/Linux side of the link instead
$ netdryrun run srl-ld
Netdryrun 0.3.1: 7 checks from srl-ld/netdryrun.yml
Deploying lab ndr-docs-srlld (2 nodes); this usually takes 30-90 s, longer the first time images are pulled...
  [PASS] srl1: BGP session to 10.0.100.2 is established -- state is established (14.4s)
  ...
  [PASS] srl1: BGP best path for 192.168.20.0/24 has as-path '65020', local-pref 100, next hop 10.0.100.2 -- best path: as-path '65020', next hop 10.0.100.2, local-pref 100, MED 0, communities none (held 11s, 3 samples) (10.6s)
Scenario: srl1-frr1 link fails
Destroying lab...
ERROR: failure scenarios on SR Linux nodes (srl1) are not supported yet; take the link down on the FRR/Linux side of the link instead
```

Fix: take down the other end of the same link. For `examples/srl-frr`, the link is `srl1:e1-1` to `frr1:eth1`:

```yaml
scenarios:
  - name: srl1-frr1 link fails
    link_down: {node: frr1, interface: eth1}
```

The effect on the network is the same: the link is down for both sides. `node_isolated` on an SR Linux node fails the same way; isolate its neighbors' links instead.

## MCP tool calls time out in the client

`dry_run` deploys a lab, so it takes 30 seconds to several minutes. Many MCP clients give up on a tool call sooner. Reproduced with the Python MCP SDK (mcp 2.3.0), `dry_run` on `my-lab` and a 20-second client timeout:

```text
MCPError: Request 'tools/call' timed out
```

With a 300-second timeout, the same call returned the full result (`"status": "passed"`) after 41 seconds.

When the client gives up, it usually stops the server. From 0.3.1, the server then destroys the lab before it exits: in the run above, the lab's three containers were up when the call timed out and gone a few seconds later, before the client had exited. 0.3.0 and earlier left the lab running. A server killed without a chance to clean up (`SIGKILL`) still leaves it; the next `dry_run` on that lab then refuses to deploy (see [a lab named X is already running](#a-lab-named-x-is-already-running)) until you destroy it with `containerlab destroy -t my-lab/topology.clab.yml --cleanup`.

Fixes:

- **Raise the client's tool timeout** to at least 5 minutes. In Claude Code, set `MCP_TOOL_TIMEOUT` (milliseconds) before starting it, for example `MCP_TOOL_TIMEOUT=600000 claude`. For other clients, look for a tool-call or request timeout setting.
- **Make the lab faster.** Lower `timeout` in `netdryrun.yml` so a broken change fails sooner, and pull images in advance so the first call does not wait on a download.
- **If the client cannot wait that long**, let the agent run `netdryrun run <folder>` in a shell and read `netdryrun-report.json`.

## No PR comment on a big lab

GitHub rejects a comment longer than 65,536 characters. From 0.3.1, the Markdown report (the PR comment and the job summary) stays under that: failed checks come first, and once the table would pass about 65,000 characters it stops with one row that says how many it left out. For a run of 1,500 checks, 5 of them failed, the 0.3.1 report code produced 64,845 characters: the 5 failures and 763 passed checks, then

```text
| | … 732 more checks (0 failed, 732 passed) | not shown: too many for one comment; all are in the JSON report | |
```

The JSON report and the job status always have every check. If the left-out rows matter to your reviewers, trim the file to the checks that matter, or split it into several `netdryrun.yml` files run as a [matrix](github-action.md#several-labs).

0.3.0 and earlier listed every check in the comment, about 90 characters each, so above roughly 700 checks GitHub rejected it: the job log said `could not comment on the PR (needs permissions pull-requests: write ...)` even though the permission was set. The verdict, the job status and the reports were not affected.

## Inconclusive: the lab never came up

Exit code `3` means checks failed, but the lab never reached a testable state, so the result says nothing about your change. Reproduced by turning off `bgpd` in the FRR `daemons` file of a copy of `examples/frr-bgp`, with `timeout: 30` and its failure scenario removed:

```text
$ netdryrun run . --json report.json
Netdryrun 0.3.1: 7 checks from netdryrun.yml
Deploying lab ndr-docs-nobgp (3 nodes); this usually takes 30-90 s, longer the first time images are pulled...
  [FAIL] r1: BGP session to 10.0.12.2 is established -- error: `vtysh -c show bgp neighbors json` failed on r1 (rc=1): bgpd is not running (33.1s)
  [FAIL] r1: BGP session to 10.0.13.2 is established -- error: `vtysh -c show bgp neighbors json` failed on r1 (rc=1): bgpd is not running (33.1s)
  [FAIL] r1: route 192.168.3.0/24 via bgp is present -- error: `vtysh -c show bgp ipv4 unicast 192.168.3.0/24 json` failed on r1 (rc=1): bgpd is not running (33.1s)
  [FAIL] r1: ping 192.168.3.1 from 192.168.1.1 expects success -- 0/3 replies (need 2) (33.1s)
warning: r1 never returned BGP state; its post-convergence checks start without the BGP gate
Convergence checks done; settling 10s before post-convergence checks...
  [FAIL] r1: prefixes from 10.0.12.2 >= 1 and <= 10 -- error: `vtysh -c show bgp neighbors json` failed on r1 (rc=1): bgpd is not running (30.1s)
  [FAIL] r1: BGP best path for 192.168.2.0/24 has as-path '65002', next hop 10.0.12.2 -- error: `vtysh -c show bgp ipv4 unicast 192.168.2.0/24 json` failed on r1 (rc=1): bgpd is not running (0.1s)
  [FAIL] r1: route 0.0.0.0/0 via bgp is absent -- error: `vtysh -c show bgp ipv4 unicast 0.0.0.0/0 json` failed on r1 (rc=1): bgpd is not running (0.1s)
Destroying lab...
INCONCLUSIVE: the lab did not reach a testable state: r1 never returned usable BGP state (r1: error: `vtysh -c show bgp neighbors json` failed on r1 (rc=1): bgpd is not running), and no check passed on any sample. Rerun with a longer timeout, or check that the lab boots (7 of 7 checks failed; this says nothing about the change)
  wrote json report: report.json
```

The run took 111 seconds. With the failure scenario left in, 0.3.1 doesn't get to this verdict: after the main checks it stops at the scenario with exit code `2` and [could not read BGP state on r1](#could-not-read-bgp-state-to-find-the-sessions-over-the-links), because it can't see which sessions the fault would take down. Either way the run is never `passed`.

The JSON report has the same text in `inconclusive_reason`, and every unready sample in `history` is marked:

```json
{"t": 33.1, "passed": false, "detail": "error: `vtysh -c show bgp neighbors json` failed on r1 (rc=1): bgpd is not running", "unready": true}
```

How it differs from the other results:

- **`error` (exit `2`):** the run could not start or finish: a config error, a missing tool, a failed deploy, a fault that did not take effect.
- **`failed` (exit `1`):** the lab was up and something is wrong. A configured BGP session that is down (an ASN typo, as in [the lab never converges](#the-lab-never-converges-timeout)) is `failed`, not `inconclusive`.
- **`inconclusive` (exit `3`):** no positive check passed on any sample, and every failed check is on a node whose CLI or BGP never answered.

Fix: check that the lab boots (`containerlab inspect`, `docker logs <container>`), that the routing daemon is enabled, and that `timeout` is long enough for slow NOSes, then rerun. One known limit: a change that deletes a node's whole BGP config looks the same and is reported `inconclusive`. It is still never `passed`. See the [full rules](reference/cli.md#when-a-run-is-inconclusive).

## Still stuck

Run with `--keep-on-failure`, look inside the nodes with `docker exec`, and read the JSON report (`--json report.json`): every check keeps the raw commands and output. If it looks like a bug, [open an issue](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/issues) with the report attached. See [Support](support.md).


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/faq/

# FAQ

## Does Netdryrun touch my production network?

No. Netdryrun™ only builds labs with containerlab on the machine where it runs, runs commands only inside the lab containers (with `docker exec`), and destroys the lab. Most are read-only show commands; the others take links down and up for failure scenarios, add and remove routes for `inject_routes` scenarios, and run any `setup` commands you write. It has no command, option or MCP tool that connects to a real device or pushes config anywhere. You apply the change to production yourself, with your normal process, after the test passes.

## What does a pass prove?

A pass means every check in your `netdryrun.yml` held in a lab running real routing software: positive checks reached the expected state within the timeout, and negative checks held for the hold time after convergence. It is strong evidence that the change does what you intended at the protocol and policy level.

It does not prove:

- **anything you did not check.** A pass covers the checks that exist. A leak with no negative check for it passes.
- **vendor or version behavior.** FRR, SR Linux, SONiC VS and cEOS are not your production routers or images.
- **scale, hardware or timing.** A lab has a few nodes and small tables, no ASICs, and different convergence times.

See [what a lab cannot prove](trust.md#what-a-lab-cannot-prove). The [verdict corpus](corpus.md) shows where Netdryrun was right and wrong on 30 realistic changes.

## What does "inconclusive" mean?

A run is `inconclusive` (exit code `3`) when checks failed but the lab never reached a state where they mean anything, for example a node whose BGP daemon never started. It says nothing about the change, good or bad: rerun, raise `timeout`, or check that the lab boots. Don't change the network change because of it, and don't apply it either: only `passed` means go.

The rules are conservative. A configured session that is down, a missing route or a failed ping is always `failed`, because an ASN typo looks exactly like a slow lab from the outside. See [when a run is inconclusive](reference/cli.md#when-a-run-is-inconclusive) and [troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md#inconclusive-the-lab-never-came-up).

## How is it different from Batfish or pyATS?

- **Batfish** models configs without booting anything. It is fast, covers many vendors and large networks, and answers broad questions. Netdryrun runs the real routing software, so it sees what the implementation actually does, on fewer nodes.
- **pyATS / Genie** is a full Python test framework with many parsers, for labs and production devices. Netdryrun is a YAML file of checks and a CLI, aimed at one job: a pass/fail gate in CI.

They work together. See [When to use what](when-to-use-what.md) for a longer, neutral comparison.

## Which network operating systems are supported?

FRR, Nokia SR Linux, SONiC (docker-sonic-vs) and Arista EOS (cEOS, bring your own image). Labs can mix them: the examples pair each one with FRR. See [drivers](reference/config.md#drivers) for what each driver supports.

## Why not Cisco or Juniper?

Their lab images are licensed. Netdryrun's CI and examples must run for anyone, so every image they use has to be free to pull: FRR, SR Linux and SONiC VS are. Arista cEOS is free to download with an account but can't be redistributed, so its example needs you to import your own image.

Cisco and Juniper images (for example IOS XRd, Cisco 8000 emulator, cRPD, vJunos) need an account, a license or both, and several are virtual machines that containerlab runs through vrnetlab. Drivers for them are on the roadmap, following the same bring-your-own-image model as cEOS. If you need one, say so in an [issue](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/issues).

## Does it work on Windows?

Yes, through WSL2. containerlab needs Linux, so install Docker and containerlab inside a WSL2 distribution (Ubuntu 22.04 is what we test on) and run Netdryrun there. Keep labs on the Linux filesystem (`~/...`) rather than under `/mnt/c`: it is faster, and SR Linux cannot save its config on a Windows drive. Netdryrun works around the second problem; see [troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md#sr-linux-fails-on-a-windows-drive-mntc). All the outputs in this documentation were produced on WSL2.

## How much memory and CPU does it need?

Memory used per node once the lab is up, measured with `docker stats` on WSL2 (20 cores, 16 GB):

| Node | Image | Memory |
|---|---|---|
| FRR | `quay.io/frrouting/frr:10.4.1` | 23 to 25 MiB |
| SONiC VS | `docker-sonic-vs:latest` | 302 MiB |
| Arista cEOS | `ceos:4.36.3M` | 903 MiB |
| Nokia SR Linux | `ghcr.io/nokia/srlinux:26.7.2` | 1.9 GB (1,947,377,664 bytes, read from the container's cgroup `memory.current`, because `docker stats` shows 0 for SR Linux) |

CPU is busy only while nodes boot. Once up, FRR and SONiC used about 1% of one core or less; cEOS was using about one full core when measured, shortly after boot.

Plan for the sum of your nodes plus a few hundred MB for Docker and containerlab. A small FRR lab runs on any laptop. A lab with several SR Linux or cEOS nodes needs a machine with 8 GB or more. GitHub-hosted `ubuntu-latest` runners have enough memory for every example.

### A 20-node lab

These numbers come from one-off runs on the maintainer's machine. The topology, the recorded checks and the reports are not published yet, so treat them as a rough guide rather than evidence you can check.

Measured on 2026-10-27 on the same WSL2 machine, images already pulled: a leaf-spine fabric of 4 spines and 16 leaves, all FRR 10.4.1, 64 links, eBGP on every link with ECMP. `netdryrun record` turned the running lab into 560 checks (128 sessions, 128 prefix counts, 304 routes) in 11 seconds. Then `netdryrun run` on those 560 checks:

| Phase | Time |
|---|---|
| Deploy (containerlab, 20 nodes) | 9 s |
| BGP converged everywhere (polled once a second) | 9 s after deploy |
| 432 convergence checks done | 25 s after deploy |
| Settle, then 128 prefix counts held 10 s | 27 s |
| Destroy | 3 s |
| **Total, `netdryrun run`** | **65 s, all 560 passed** |

Two more runs on the same lab:

- **With a failure scenario** (spine1 isolated: 16 links down, 4 checks on leaf1): 128 s, all 564 passed. The scenario took 32 s (its checks, restoring the links, settling 10 s). Proving that all 432 convergence checks recovered afterwards took another 32 s.
- **With a broken change** (leaf16 stops announcing its LAN): 193 s, 83 failed, exactly the expected ones: the 19 routes to that LAN, the 60 leaf prefix counts that dropped from 15 to 14, and the 4 spine prefix counts that dropped from 1 to 0. The prefix counts failed within 31 s. The missing routes failed at 120 s, the `timeout` that `record` writes, so most of a failing run is that wait. Lower `timeout` if your lab converges faster.

Memory: 532 MiB for the 20 nodes at the peak (25 MiB per leaf, up to 58 MiB per spine with 16 BGP sessions), about 1 GB more host memory in use during the run, and 72 MB for Netdryrun itself. Netdryrun used a bit more than one core while polling.

At this size each polling round takes 9 to 12 seconds instead of the nominal 3, because every check is its own `docker exec` and Netdryrun runs 8 at a time. A check therefore needs about 20 seconds to collect its two passing samples even when the network converged sooner, and failure detection is coarser. Timeouts still work as documented: a check is only failed on a failing sample after its timeout. If a big lab's runs are too slow, trim the recorded file to the checks that matter.

## How long does a run take, and what does CI cost?

On GitHub-hosted `ubuntu-latest` runners, measured from three CI runs on `main` on 2026-10-27, before 0.3.0 added a few checks per example:

| CI job | What it does | Time |
|---|---|---|
| `e2e (frr-bgp)` | Install containerlab and Netdryrun, pull FRR, run the checks and a link-failure scenario | 100 to 107 s |
| `e2e (srl-frr)` | The same with SR Linux and FRR (the SR Linux image is 3.2 GB) | 88 to 107 s |
| `catches-bad-change` | Run `frr-bgp-broken` and expect it to fail | 54 to 66 s |
| `agent-demo` | Replay the agent demo: two full runs | 82 to 94 s |

The whole CI workflow, with these jobs in parallel, took 2 minutes 10 seconds to 2 minutes 38 seconds in the last ten successful runs.

GitHub Actions minutes are free on public repositories with standard GitHub-hosted runners. On private repositories, each job uses minutes from your plan, rounded up to the whole minute, so a job like `e2e (frr-bgp)` uses 2 minutes. See [GitHub's billing page](https://docs.github.com/en/billing/managing-billing-for-your-products/managing-billing-for-github-actions/about-billing-for-github-actions) for current prices. Netdryrun itself is free.

Local runs are faster once images are pulled; see the times on the [examples page](examples.md).

## Does it collect any data?

No. The CLI, the GitHub Action and the MCP server have no telemetry and don't phone home. Reports are written only to the files you ask for. The GitHub Action's `cloud` input is reserved for Netdryrun Cloud, a hosted service that is not available yet; setting it today uploads nothing. See [privacy](trust.md#privacy) and the [privacy notice](privacy.md).

## What is the license?

Apache-2.0, for the code. "Netdryrun" and the logo are trademarks: forks are welcome under a different name. See [Trust and security](trust.md#license).

## Where do I get help?

Read [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md) first. Then [open an issue](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/issues) with the JSON report attached. See [Support](support.md).


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/corpus/

# Network Change Verdict Corpus

How much does a typical "ping after the change" test miss? This corpus answers that with data anyone can rerun.

!!! info "How to read these numbers"
    This is a small benchmark the Netdryrun maintainers wrote: one FRR provider topology, 30 changes in v1 and 18 in v2, each labelled harmful or safe before any run. It compares testing methods on the same changes. It is **not** an independent benchmark and **not** a reliability estimate for production networks: "24/30" does not mean Netdryrun is right 80% of the time on your network. Both runs below are the rerun on the released 0.3.1 (commit `08059de`, code identical to the v0.3.1 tag), done by the release gate on 2026-10-27. The first published runs used pre-release builds (v1: commit `ec23379`, which called itself 0.2.0; v2: a development build that recorded no commit). On 0.3.1 every v1 verdict is unchanged, and v2 changed on one case: 18, now rejected as its expected verdict says. The [changes since](how-its-built.md#every-miss-and-what-it-changed) are listed per miss.

There are two runs. v1's cases and expected verdicts are frozen as first published; its results below are the 0.3.1 rerun, with the same verdicts as the first run. [Corpus v2](#corpus-v2) is a second, separately pre-registered run that makes v1's misses testable, including scenarios where a customer or peer misbehaves.

## Method

- **The network:** a small provider (AS65000, two routers) with a customer, an upstream transit and a settlement-free peer, running FRR in containerlab. Its written intent is in [INTENT.md](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/corpus/INTENT.md).
- **The changes:** 30 realistic edits ([cases](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/corpus/cases)): route leaks, filter typos, mass withdrawals, fat-fingered ASNs, latent risks, and safe changes that must not be blocked.
- **Pre-registered verdicts:** each case's expected verdict (would an experienced operator reject it?) was **committed to git before any run**. Verdicts are never edited afterwards; findings after the run are listed separately below.
- **Three strategies, same running lab per case:**
    1. **Ping only:** the customer pings the upstream and the peer.
    2. **All BGP sessions up:** every session established.
    3. **Netdryrun™ intent checks:** one [intent spec](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/corpus/specs/intent.yml), written once and used unchanged for every case, so it can't be tuned to win.
- **Rerun it:** `python corpus/run.py` on any Linux or WSL2 machine with Docker and containerlab. It uses the Netdryrun code in your checkout.
- **Rerun it on GitHub's machines:** fork the repository, then run the [Reproduce corpus](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/.github/workflows/reproduce-corpus.yml) workflow from your fork's Actions tab. It has not been run on GitHub yet, and it covers v1 only. It installs containerlab 0.81.1 and Netdryrun from your checkout (not the build that produced the committed results, so a verdict that differs can come from a code change) on a GitHub-hosted runner, runs every v1 case, uploads `results.json`, `RESULTS.md` and the run log as artifacts, and lists every verdict that differs from the committed [`results.json`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/corpus/results/results.json) in the run summary.

## Results



Generated 2026-10-27T18:00:53+00:00 with netdryrun 0.3.1, containerlab 0.81.1, FRR quay.io/frrouting/frr:10.4.1, commit `08059de`. Rerun everything with `python corpus/run.py`.

**Conflict of interest:** the Netdryrun maintainers wrote this corpus and the runner. Expected verdicts were committed before any run (see the git history of [`corpus/cases/`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/corpus/cases)). Losses are kept and shown at the same size as the catches.

## Summary (30 cases: 19 harmful, 11 safe)

| Strategy | Correct | Harmful changes caught | Approved a bad change | Blocked a good change | Errors |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ping only | **20/30** | 9/19 | 10 | 0 | 0 |
| All BGP sessions up | **15/30** | 4/19 | 15 | 0 | 0 |
| Netdryrun intent checks | **24/30** | 14/19 | 5 | 1 | 0 |

## Netdryrun's losses

- **`06-customer-adds-prefix` Customer announces a second allowed /24** (false block). Normal customer growth inside the registered range.
- **`12-ibgp-send-community-dropped` send-community removed on the pe1 to pe2 iBGP session** (false pass). A common mistake when rebuilding iBGP sessions.
- **`18-redistribute-connected` redistribute connected added on pe1** (false pass). Not covered by the intent spec, which has no check for infrastructure routes at the customer.
- **`21-customer-max-prefix-removed` Customer maximum-prefix safety limit removed** (false pass). Latent risk: no steady-state check can see it until the customer actually leaks. Catching it needs a failure-injection scenario (the customer sends many prefixes), planned for a later release.
- **`23-fat-finger-third-party-origin` pe1 accidentally originates 8.8.8.0/24** (false pass). Not covered by the intent spec, which has no check for unexpected routes at the customer.
- **`30-peer-import-filter-removed` Peer inbound filter replaced with permit-all** (false pass). Latent risk: invisible in steady state until the peer misbehaves. Needs a failure-injection scenario.

## Findings after the run

These findings came after the run. The table above is left exactly as pre-registered; nothing in [`corpus/cases/`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/corpus/cases) was edited.

**Case 12 was labeled wrong.** The case expected that removing `neighbor 10.0.3.2 send-community` on pe1 stops pe2 from seeing the customer community. In FRR (verified on 10.4.1) communities are sent to every neighbor by default, so deleting the explicit line is a no-op: `show running-config` no longer shows it, but pe1 still advertises `10.100.0.0/24` to pe2 with community `65000:100`, and pe2 still matches it (`show bgp ipv4 unicast community 65000:100` lists the route). Reproduce with `scripts/corpus_case12_verify.sh`. The change is actually safe, so all three strategies answered case 12 correctly. With that one label corrected the scores would be: ping only 21/30, sessions up 16/30, Netdryrun 25/30. The headline numbers stay at the pre-registered values. The mistake would have been real on platforms that do not send communities by default (Cisco IOS, for example); a vendor-specific version of this case belongs in a future corpus.

**Cases 18, 23, 21 and 30 are real misses.** 18 and 23 are gaps in the intent spec (no check for unexpected routes reaching the customer or the upstream). 21 and 30 are latent risks that no steady-state check can see; they need a failure-injection scenario where the customer or peer actually misbehaves. These stay as losses.



## Corpus v2

The v1 results above are frozen. Corpus v2 is a separate, second run with its own pre-registered cases. It turns v1's misses into things a test can see:

- **Unexpected routes** (v1 cases 18 and 23): the v2 intent spec says infrastructure prefixes and a sentinel list of well-known third-party prefixes must never be BGP routes at the customer, the upstream or the peer. These are `route` checks with `present: false`; no new check type is needed.
- **Latent risks** (v1 cases 21 and 30): two failure scenarios use the [`inject_routes`](reference/config.md#injecting-routes) fault, which ships in Netdryrun 0.3.1, to make a neighbor misbehave. The customer floods 200 more-specifics from its own /16, and the peer announces a more-specific of our customer's space and a third-party /24. The checks then verify that the max-prefix limit and the import filter actually hold.
- **Rigid counts** (v1 case 06): announced-prefix counts are a range (2 to 51), so customer growth inside its block is not blocked.
- **Vendor defaults** (v1 case 12): the FRR no-op is labeled safe, and the genuinely harmful variant is a separate case.

v2 changes two lines in the base lab so the customer's max-prefix limit can actually trip: in v1 the customer filter allowed at most 7 prefixes, so a limit of 100 could never be reached. The differences, the written intent (I1 to I9) and the disclosures are in [v2/INTENT.md](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/corpus/v2/INTENT.md). The spec is [v2/specs/intent.yml](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/corpus/v2/specs/intent.yml).

**Pre-registration:** all 18 cases and their expected verdicts were committed and pushed in [`322cc4e`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/commit/322cc4ede21492c3914a0a53b67268bea7abf7d6) (2026-10-27 04:02 UTC), before any v2 case was deployed. Rerun it with `python corpus/run.py --corpus v2`.

Generated 2026-10-27T19:05:43+00:00 with netdryrun 0.3.1, containerlab 0.81.1, FRR quay.io/frrouting/frr:10.4.1, commit `08059de`. Rerun everything with `python corpus/run.py --corpus v2`.

**Conflict of interest:** the Netdryrun maintainers wrote this corpus and the runner. Expected verdicts were committed before any run (see the git history of [`corpus/v2/cases/`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/corpus/v2/cases)). Losses are kept and shown at the same size as the catches.

### Summary (18 cases: 11 harmful, 7 safe)

| Strategy | Correct | Harmful changes caught | Approved a bad change | Blocked a good change | Errors |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ping only | **9/18** | 2/11 | 9 | 0 | 0 |
| All BGP sessions up | **7/18** | 0/11 | 11 | 0 | 0 |
| Netdryrun intent checks | **17/18** | 10/11 | 1 | 0 | 0 |

### Every case
