| `15-upstream-default-filtered` [Default route from the upstream filtered on import](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/corpus/v2/cases/15-upstream-default-filtered.yml) | policy-bug | unsafe | ❌ approved a bad change | ❌ approved a bad change | ✅ | I3 customer has default |
| `16-customer-session-peer-group` [Customer session moved into a CUSTOMERS peer-group](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/corpus/v2/cases/16-customer-session-peer-group.yml) | refactor | safe | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | nothing |
| `17-customer-region-community` [Add an informational region community to customer routes](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/corpus/v2/cases/17-customer-region-community.yml) | hygiene | safe | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | nothing |
| `18-aggregate-discard-route-removed` [Discard route for our aggregate deleted as unused](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/corpus/v2/cases/18-aggregate-discard-route-removed.yml) | hygiene | unsafe | ❌ approved a bad change | ❌ approved a bad change | ✅ | I2 upstream has our aggregate; I2 peer has our aggregate; I5 upstream receives 2 to 51 prefixes from us; I5 peer receives 2 to 51 prefixes from us |

### Netdryrun's losses

- **`04-redundant-aggregate-typo` Aggregate added on pe2 for redundancy, mistyped as 192.0.12.0/24** (false pass). Expected to be missed. I7 only spot-checks a few well-known prefixes, and nothing bounds what the customer receives.

### Findings after the run

These findings came after the v2 run. The table above is left exactly as pre-registered in commit `322cc4e`; nothing in [`corpus/v2/cases/`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/corpus/v2/cases) was edited.

**Run provenance.** `results.json` records the commit as `unknown`: the run used git inside WSL on a Windows git worktree, and that git could not read the worktree. The run started at 04:02:42 UTC, 16 seconds after the pre-registration commit `322cc4e`. `src/` and `corpus/run.py` were not changed during the run. The renderer, the docs and the unit tests were edited during the run, and none of them affect verdicts.

**Case 04 is a real miss, as predicted.** pe2 announced the mistyped 192.0.12.0/24 to pe1 and on to the customer, and no check looked for it. I7 only spot-checks a few well-known prefixes, and nothing bounds what the customer receives. Catching this class needs a check that the customer receives only routes from known origins, or only expected prefixes from our own AS. No such check type exists yet.

**Case 18 is a real miss.** With the discard route deleted, FRR (traditional defaults, no `bgp network import-check`) kept announcing 192.0.2.0/24, so I2 passed. The harm is the routing loop for unused addresses inside the aggregate, which no check probes. A `ping` with `expect: failure` to an unused address in 192.0.2.0/24 from the upstream would not show the loop either, because ping fails both with and without it. Catching it needs a path or traceroute check (TTL exceeded versus a clean discard).

**Ping only's catch of case 14 is partly a lab artifact.** In the lab, the customer's BGP default is not active, because containerlab's management default route outranks it (the spec checks the default with `active: false` for this reason). Once the customer lost its specific routes, its pings had no path at all. A real customer with a working default would still ping, and the ping baseline would pass the change. The result stays as measured.

**Rerun on the released 0.3.1 (2026-10-27, by the release gate):** every verdict matches the first run except case 18 (`18-aggregate-discard-route-removed`). The development build approved it; 0.3.1 rejects it, which is the pre-registered expected verdict, because the upstream and the peer no longer receive the aggregate (checks I2 and I5 fail). 0.3.1 changed how routes are read (received paths count, errors are never read as "no routes"), and this case was one of v2's two misses. Netdryrun is now 17/18 on v2. The cases and the expected verdicts are unchanged.


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/how-its-built/

# How Netdryrun is built and verified

A tool that approves network changes has to earn trust with evidence, not claims. Most of this page links to something you can inspect or rerun yourself: the test corpus, the CI runs, the commit history and the release pipeline. Where a claim can't be checked yet, the page says so.

## At a glance

| | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Accuracy on realistic BGP changes | Verdict Corpus v1: **24/30** (ping only 20/30, sessions up 15/30). v2: **17/18** (ping only 9/18, sessions up 7/18). Both ran on the released 0.3.1 (the release gate reruns them for every release). [Results](corpus.md) |
| Expected verdicts fixed before any run | Committed first, never edited: [`b4df0b0`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/commit/b4df0b0) (v1), [`322cc4e`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/commit/322cc4e) (v2) |
| Results you can rerun | One command locally (`python corpus/run.py`, `--corpus v2` for v2). The [Reproduce corpus](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/.github/workflows/reproduce-corpus.yml) workflow reruns v1 from your own fork; it has not been run on GitHub yet |
| Real labs on every change | FRR and Nokia SR Linux labs boot in CI on every push and pull request ([runs](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/actions/workflows/ci.yml)) |
| What users install is tested too | The released Action and the PyPI package, on every push and weekly ([`published-action.yml`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/.github/workflows/published-action.yml)) |
| Supply chain | PyPI Trusted Publishing, CodeQL, OpenSSF Scorecard, every Action pinned to a commit |
| Losses | Published next to the wins, never removed |

## Engineering process

Netdryrun is developed by its maintainer, Victor Khen, with AI-assisted tooling. The maintainer sets the direction, reviews the results, decides what ships and publishes every release. Every change, whoever or whatever wrote it, goes through the same CI tests and lab runs, and every release through the release gate described below. The [commit history](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/commits/main) records every change.

## Pre-registered accuracy testing

The [Verdict Corpus](corpus.md) measures Netdryrun on realistic BGP changes, each labelled harmful or safe in advance, and compares it with two common checks: "ping still works" and "all BGP sessions are up".

- **Verdicts are committed before anything runs.** v1: all 30 cases with their expected verdicts in [`b4df0b0`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/commit/b4df0b0), results later in [`7576298`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/commit/7576298). v2: 18 new cases in [`322cc4e`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/commit/322cc4e), results later in [`669b30f`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/commit/669b30f). No case was edited after a run ([history of `corpus/cases/`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/commits/main/corpus/cases)).
- **The tool was run on the corpus during development, and changed before the published runs.** During 0.2.0 development, runs against the v1 cases found a bug (a change that broke a baseline check ended a scenario run as `error`) and showed that the new polling made the corpus 2 to 3 times faster; both are in the [changelog](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md). The expected verdicts were not changed; the v1 intent spec changed by one comment line.
- **Both published runs were rerun on the released 0.3.1** by the release gate (commit `08059de`, code identical to the v0.3.1 tag). The first runs used pre-release builds: v1 on commit `ec23379` (it called itself 0.2.0, before the tagged 0.2.0), v2 on a development build that recorded no commit. On 0.3.1 every v1 verdict is the same; v2 changed on case 18 (now rejected, as expected), recorded in [AMENDMENTS.md](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/corpus/v2/AMENDMENTS.md).
- **v2 is a harder test, not a friendlier one.** Its cases target the kinds of change v1 missed. It was written after seeing v1's results, which is a limitation to keep in mind.
- **Everything reruns.** The runner ([`corpus/run.py`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/corpus/run.py)), every case and the raw output ([`results.json`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/corpus/results/results.json)) are public. `python corpus/run.py` reruns v1 and `--corpus v2` reruns v2, with the code you have checked out (so a different verdict can come from a code change, not only from noise). The GitHub workflow reruns v1 the same way on a hosted runner and lists any verdict that differs; it has not been run on GitHub yet, and it does not cover v2.
- **Limit of this evidence:** git commit dates come from the author's machine. The history proves the order of the commits and that the cases were not changed; it is not an independent timestamp.

## Every miss, and what it changed

A test you always pass tells you nothing. Netdryrun's misses stay in the published results, at the same size as its catches, and each one has driven a specific improvement.


**Verdict Corpus v1: wrong on 6 of 30 cases.** It approved 5 harmful changes and blocked 1 safe one ([RESULTS.md](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/corpus/RESULTS.md)).


**Verdict Corpus v2: wrong on 1 of 18 cases on 0.3.1**, a harmful change approved. The first run, on a development build, was wrong on 2 ([v2 results](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/corpus/v2/RESULTS.md)).

| Case | Outcome | Root cause | What changed | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| v1 [06](corpus/06-customer-adds-prefix.md): customer announces a second allowed /24 | Blocked a safe change | The intent spec pinned exactly 2 prefixes towards the upstream and peer, so normal customer growth looked like a leak | v2 checks a range (2 to 51 prefixes); the growth cases 07 and 08 pass | Fixed |
| v1 [12](corpus/12-ibgp-send-community-dropped.md): send-community removed on iBGP | Approved | **Our label was wrong.** On FRR, communities are sent by default, so the change is a no-op ([AMENDMENTS.md](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/corpus/AMENDMENTS.md), with a reproduction script) | Scored as a loss anyway, never corrected in our favour. v2 case 09 tests the corrected expectation and case 10 the truly harmful variant; both judged correctly | Label error |
| v1 [18](corpus/18-redistribute-connected.md): redistribute connected on pe1 | Approved | Spec gap: nothing checked for infrastructure routes leaving the AS | New intent I6: no link or loopback routes at the customer, upstream or peer. v2 case 02 (the same mistake on pe2) caught | Fixed |
| v1 [23](corpus/23-fat-finger-third-party-origin.md): pe1 originates 8.8.8.0/24 | Approved | Spec gap: nothing checked for third-party space | New intent I7, a sentinel list of well-known prefixes. v2 case 03 caught | Partly fixed (see v2 04) |
| v1 [21](corpus/21-customer-max-prefix-removed.md): customer max-prefix removed | Approved | Latent risk, invisible until the customer misbehaves | New `inject_routes` failure scenario: the customer floods 200 prefixes. v2 cases 05 and 11 caught | Fixed (the scenario ships in 0.3.1) |
| v1 [30](corpus/30-peer-import-filter-removed.md): peer inbound filter replaced with permit-all | Approved | Latent risk, invisible until the peer misbehaves | The same scenario type, with the peer announcing routes it does not own. v2 case 06 caught | Fixed (the scenario ships in 0.3.1) |
| v2 04: redundant aggregate mistyped as 192.0.12.0/24 | Approved | I7 checks only a few well-known prefixes; nothing bounds what the customer receives | Predicted as a likely miss in the case file before the run | Open |
| v2 18: discard route for the aggregate deleted | Approved on the development build; **rejected on 0.3.1** | Causes a routing loop for unused addresses inside the aggregate; no check sends traffic there | 0.3.1 reads received paths and never reads an error as "no routes": the upstream and the peer no longer receive the aggregate, so checks I2 and I5 fail. The loop itself is still not probed; a path or traceroute check would show it | Caught on 0.3.1 (not by probing the loop) |

Two caveats apply. v2 was written after seeing v1's misses, so its improvements are measured on cases designed by the same team. And the corpus runs on FRR only, with one topology.

## Continuous integration with live labs

Every push to `main` and every pull request runs [`ci.yml`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/.github/workflows/ci.yml) ([runs](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/actions/workflows/ci.yml)): unit tests on Python 3.10, 3.12 and 3.13, plus three jobs that boot real containerlab labs.

- **`e2e`** runs the GitHub Action on [`examples/frr-bgp`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples/frr-bgp) and [`examples/srl-frr`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples/srl-frr) (FRR and Nokia SR Linux). Both must pass.
- **`catches-bad-change`** runs [`examples/frr-bgp-broken`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples/frr-bgp-broken), a change that leaks a default route. The job succeeds only if Netdryrun rejects it.
- **`agent-demo`** replays [`examples/agent-demo`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/examples/agent-demo): a route-leaking change must fail on exactly the leak guards, and the proper fix must pass.

A second workflow, [`published-action.yml`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/.github/workflows/published-action.yml), tests what users install rather than the code on `main`: the released Action by its tag (it must pass a good change and reject a bad one), and `pip install` and `uvx` from PyPI on every supported Python version, including an MCP handshake.

SONiC and Arista EOS are not in CI yet (cEOS is an image each user downloads from Arista). Their unit tests parse output captured from real lab runs ([`tests/fixtures`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/tree/main/tests/fixtures)).

Every release also goes through a seven-layer release gate, from linting and mutation testing of the verdict logic to chaos runs on the built package, described in [RELEASING.md](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/RELEASING.md); from the next release on, each release's results are committed in `releases/<version>/GATE.md`.

## Performance on a 20-node fabric

On a 20-node leaf-spine fabric (4 spines, 16 leaves, FRR, 64 links), `netdryrun record` produced 560 checks in 11 seconds, and a full `netdryrun run` (deploy, convergence, all checks, destroy) took 65 seconds. A deliberately broken change failed exactly the 83 checks it should have. Full numbers, memory use and limits are in the [FAQ](faq.md#a-20-node-lab). These come from one-off runs on the maintainer's machine; the topology and the reports are not published yet, so you can't check them the way you can check the corpus.

## Cross-model review (not a human audit)

Before releases 0.1.0 and 0.2.0, the code was also reviewed by AI models from other vendors (OpenAI GPT and xAI Grok); 0.3.0 was not. Separate agent sessions that start without the author's context also review changes. These review outputs are not published. Fixes from these reviews: [`ec23379`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/commit/ec23379) (v0.2.0), [`6495759`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/commit/6495759) (agent demo) and [`90fe0ae`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/commit/90fe0ae): a security review of the MCP server, the GitHub Action and every path where lab output reaches a shell, a device CLI or a PR comment, with 7 findings, each fixed with a regression test.

These reviewers are AI models, not human auditors. No independent human security audit has been done yet. Report vulnerabilities through the [security policy](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/security/policy).

## Defects found by our own testing

Each was found by running Netdryrun against live labs or the corpus, and is recorded in the [changelog](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).

- **False passes on SR Linux and Arista (fixed):** a leaked route that was received but not installed was invisible, so a `present: false` check passed when it should have failed. Fixed in [`77f43d6`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/commit/77f43d6), with regression tests on captured output ([`test_drivers.py`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/tests/test_drivers.py)).
- **Wrong status after a failure scenario (fixed):** a change that broke a baseline check ended as `error` instead of `failed`. Found with [`scripts/pack_verify.sh`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/scripts/pack_verify.sh); fixed in [`f6ea560`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/commit/f6ea560).
- **PR comments over GitHub's size limit on large labs (fixed):** found by the 20-node scale test. From 0.3.1, the comment is cut to fit GitHub's limit, failures first, and says how many checks it left out; the JSON and JUnit reports keep every check.
- **A mislabeled corpus case:** [case 12](corpus/12-ibgp-send-community-dropped.md), above.

## Supply-chain security

- **Releases** are published to PyPI with Trusted Publishing, so no tokens are stored ([`release.yml`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/.github/workflows/release.yml)). A release fails if the tag and the package version differ.
- **OpenSSF Scorecard** rates the repository's practices weekly and on every push ([current score](https://scorecard.dev/viewer/?uri=github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun)), including the checks where it scores low today; the viewer lists each one.
- **CodeQL** scans the Python code and the workflows ([`codeql.yml`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/.github/workflows/codeql.yml)).
- **Every third-party GitHub Action is pinned to a commit**, in the workflows and in [`action.yml`](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/action.yml). Dependabot keeps the pins current.

## What we do not claim

- **Not production safety.** A pass means the change behaved correctly in a lab running open-source or lab images of network operating systems. It does not prove the change is safe on your network ([what a lab cannot prove](trust.md#what-a-lab-cannot-prove)).
- **Not Internet scale.** The largest measured lab has 20 nodes and small routing tables. Nothing here is tested with full Internet tables or hundreds of peers.
- **Not vendor parity.** FRR, SR Linux, SONiC and cEOS behave differently from each other and from hardware routers. The corpus runs only on FRR, with one topology and one intent spec per version, all written by the Netdryrun maintainers.


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/when-to-use-what/

# When to use what

Several good open-source tools help you test network changes. They answer different questions and work well together. This page tries to describe each one fairly; if something here is wrong or out of date, please [open an issue](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/issues).

## The short version

| Tool | Best at | Runs routers? |
|---|---|---|
| [Batfish](https://batfish.org) | Analyzing configs of many vendors without booting anything: reachability, ACLs and firewall rules, routing, differences between two snapshots | No, it models them |
| [pyATS / Genie](https://developer.cisco.com/pyats/) | A full Python test framework with a large library of device parsers, for testing labs and real (including production) devices, with state snapshots and diffs | Works against any reachable device |
| [containerlab](https://containerlab.dev) | Running container-based network labs from a YAML topology, for many network operating systems | Yes, it is the lab |
| Your own scripts | Exactly the checks your team needs, around a lab you already run, with no new dependency | Yes, through containerlab |
| Netdryrun™ | Declarative, convergence-aware checks on a containerlab lab, packaged for CI with a pass/fail verdict and evidence | Yes, through containerlab |

## Batfish

Batfish parses device configs and builds a model of the network's control and data plane. Because nothing has to boot, it is fast, covers large networks, and supports configs from many vendors. It can answer broad questions ("can any host in this subnet reach that server?", "what changed between these two snapshots?") that are hard to test by sending packets.

Use it when you want broad, fast analysis on every commit, especially for ACLs, firewall policy and multi-vendor configs that you cannot run in containers.

A model is not the running software, so behavior that depends on the real implementation (timers, convergence order, bugs) is outside what it sees. That is where a lab helps.

## pyATS / Genie

pyATS is a mature Python test framework from Cisco, and Genie adds a large library of parsers and models that turn CLI output into structured data. It can learn the state of a device, take before and after snapshots, and diff them. It works against lab devices and real ones.

Use it when you need deep, programmable testing, broad parser coverage (especially for Cisco platforms), or pre- and post-change checks on production devices.

Netdryrun is narrower: a YAML file and a GitHub Action, with no test code to write, and it only runs against labs. If you already have pyATS tests, keep them.

## containerlab

containerlab runs network labs from a YAML topology: container-native network operating systems (such as Nokia SR Linux, Arista cEOS, Juniper cRPD, FRR) and, through vrnetlab, many VM-based ones. It handles wiring, management addresses and lifecycle.

Use it whenever you want a real lab on a laptop or a CI runner. Netdryrun does not replace it; Netdryrun drives it.

## Your own scripts around containerlab

Many teams already run containerlab in CI with a script that deploys the lab, sleeps, runs a few `show` commands or pings, and tears down. That is free, flexible, and needs no new tool. If your checks are few and your lab rarely changes, keep it.

Scripts tend to get harder in the same places, and those are what Netdryrun packages:

- **Timing.** A fixed `sleep` either wastes minutes or fails while BGP is still converging. Netdryrun polls until each check passes twice in a row, and runs "must never happen" checks only after convergence, for a hold window.
- **Routes that hide.** A leaked route that was received but not selected doesn't show in the main routing table output on every network OS. Netdryrun's drivers read where each one keeps it (FRR, SR Linux, SONiC, cEOS).
- **Evidence.** One verdict, an exit code, JUnit, a PR comment, and a JSON file with every command and its raw output, instead of a log to read.
- **Scenarios and agents.** Link-down and node-isolation scenarios with recovery checks, and an MCP server so an AI agent can run the same checks.

The two mix well: keep a script for anything Netdryrun doesn't check, and call `netdryrun check` from it for the rest.

## Netdryrun

Netdryrun adds a test layer on top of a containerlab lab:

- positive checks wait for convergence and must pass twice in a row
- negative checks (absent routes, failing pings, prefix upper bounds) run only after convergence and must hold
- a route that was received but not selected counts as present
- every run produces one pass/fail result, a CI-friendly exit code, and a JSON evidence file


Version 0.3.1 has drivers for FRR, Nokia SR Linux, SONiC and Arista EOS (bring your own cEOS image), and its checks cover BGP sessions, prefix counts, routes, BGP best-path attributes and ping, with link-down, node-isolation and route-injection (FRR only) failure scenarios.

It does not do static analysis, build labs for you, or test production devices.

## How they combine

A reasonable pipeline uses more than one:

1. **Batfish** on every commit for fast, broad config analysis.
2. A **containerlab** topology that mirrors the change.
3. **Netdryrun** in CI to boot that lab, wait for convergence, and gate the merge on runtime behavior.
4. **pyATS / Genie** (or similar) for pre- and post-change checks on the production devices during the change window.

None of these steps proves the change is safe on its own. Each one removes a different class of mistakes.

[Batfish, then Netdryrun](batfish.md) shows steps 1 and 3 together on a small FRR network, with measured times. In that test, Batfish caught two of three bad changes in seconds, before any lab booted; the third depended on an FRR default that only the running routers showed.


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/trust/

# Trust and security

## License

Netdryrun™ is open source under the [Apache License 2.0](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/LICENSE). The source is at [github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun).

## How releases are published

- Releases are built and published by a GitHub Actions workflow when a version tag (`v*`) is pushed. The workflow checks that the tag matches the package version before building.
- Packages are uploaded to [PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/netdryrun/) with **Trusted Publishing** (OpenID Connect). No PyPI token or password is stored in the repository or its secrets; PyPI accepts the upload because it comes from that workflow in that repository.
- The same workflow creates a GitHub release with the built files attached.
- The GitHub Action (`netdryrun/netdryrun@v0.3.1`) installs Netdryrun from the action's own source at the tag you reference. Pin a tag or a commit SHA.

## Reporting a security issue

Email **[security@netdryrun.com](mailto:security@netdryrun.com)**. Please do not open a public issue for a vulnerability. Include the version, what you found, and how to reproduce it.

Past advisories: [0.3.0 could pass a check without testing what the file said](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/advisories/0.3.0-false-pass/README.md), found by our own audit and fixed in 0.3.1, with a rerunnable test for each path. 0.3.0 is yanked on PyPI.

## What a lab cannot prove

A Netdryrun pass means the change behaved correctly in a lab. The lab runs real routing software, so a pass is strong evidence for protocol logic and policy intent: sessions come up, the intended prefixes are accepted, routes land in the routing table, traffic gets through, and unwanted routes stay out. It does not prove:

- **Vendor-specific behavior.** Open-source and container routers (FRR, SR Linux, SONiC VS) are not your vendor's routers, and even Arista cEOS is not the same as EOS on hardware. Defaults, policy evaluation and bugs differ between implementations and versions. For Arista you can bring your own licensed cEOS image.
- **Scale.** A lab has a handful of nodes and small tables, not full Internet tables or hundreds of peers.
- **Hardware and ASIC behavior.** Containers have no forwarding hardware, so TCAM limits, hardware programming and line-rate effects are not tested.
- **Timing at scale.** Convergence time in a small lab says little about convergence time in a large production network.


Version 0.3.1 also covers only BGP (IPv4/IPv6 unicast), routes, BGP best-path attributes and ping, plus link-down, node-isolation and route-injection (FRR only) failure scenarios. OSPF/IS-IS adjacencies and path checks are not covered yet.


## Running untrusted labs

containerlab runs privileged containers, so a topology and its configs are code that runs with root on the host. Only run labs you trust. In CI, see the [GitHub Action security notes](github-action.md#security-notes). For AI agents, see the [MCP safety model](ai-agents.md#safety-model).

What follows from that, by design:

- **`netdryrun.yml` is code too.** `nodes.<node>.setup` commands are shell commands run inside the node, and a `netdryrun.yml` can point at a topology in any folder. Review a `netdryrun.yml` the way you review a topology.
- **Everything else in `netdryrun.yml` is data.** From 0.3.1, VRF and interface names are restricted to letters, digits and a few punctuation marks before they reach a device CLI, and addresses and prefixes must parse as IP. A check can't run a device command it doesn't name.
- **`as_path_regex` runs with no time limit.** A pathological pattern can stall a run until your CI job's timeout; it can't do anything else. Set `timeout-minutes` on the job.
- **Text from a lab is treated as untrusted** wherever it ends up (0.3.1 and later): escaped in PR comments and step summaries, kept to one comment line in a recorded baseline, and flattened and capped in MCP results.

## Privacy

**The tool has no telemetry.** The CLI, the GitHub Action and the MCP server do not phone home or send usage data anywhere. Reports are written only to the files you ask for (and to the GitHub Actions step summary when running in Actions). containerlab and Docker may pull images from registries named in your topology, as they normally would.

The GitHub Action has a `cloud` input reserved for a future hosted service, Netdryrun Cloud. **Netdryrun Cloud is not available yet**: its address doesn't exist, so setting `cloud: true` today uploads nothing and only adds an "evidence upload failed" warning. If it launches, uploading will stay opt-in, and its privacy terms will be published first. Leave `cloud` off.

**No AI inside the tool.** The CLI, the GitHub Action and the MCP server contain no AI model and call no AI service; verdicts come from checks run against your lab. When an AI agent uses the MCP server, the agent sends whatever it chooses to the model provider *you* picked; Netdryrun is not part of that path.

**AI in how we build it.** Development is done with Anthropic's Claude. Releases 0.1.0 and 0.2.0 were also reviewed by OpenAI and xAI models ([how it's built](how-its-built.md)). If you are a [design partner](design-partners.md), the sanitized configs you send us are processed with Anthropic's Claude to build your lab, under terms that don't allow training on them, and with no other AI service. They are deleted within 30 days after delivery unless you ask us to keep them. There are no paid products yet. See the [privacy notice](privacy.md#configs-you-send-us).

**This website** is static documentation hosted on GitHub Pages. It sets no cookies, has no analytics and no forms, and serves its fonts itself, so your browser contacts no third party. GitHub, as the host, receives your IP address and request details to serve the pages.

## Trademarks

"Netdryrun" and the Netdryrun logos are trademarks of the Netdryrun project. The Apache-2.0 license covers the code, not the name: forks are welcome under a different name. See the [trademark policy](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/TRADEMARKS.md).


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/support/

# Support and versioning policy

## Support

Netdryrun is free open-source software under Apache-2.0, provided as is. Support for free use is best effort through [GitHub issues](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/issues). Security reports get priority (see [Contact](contact.md)). There is no uptime or response-time guarantee for free use.

Only the latest release gets fixes. Upgrading is the fix for bugs in older releases.

## Version numbers

Netdryrun uses [semantic versioning](https://semver.org). Before 1.0, a minor release (0.2 to 0.3) may contain breaking changes; patch releases (0.2.0 to 0.2.1) never do. Every change is in the [changelog](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).

## What counts as a breaking change

These are the interfaces other tools and agents rely on:

| Interface | Stable contract |
|---|---|
| CLI | command names, flags, and exit codes (`0` passed, `1` failed, `2` error, `3` inconclusive) |
| `netdryrun.yml` | check types and keys; a file that validated keeps validating |
| JSON report | the `schema` field (`netdryrun.report/v1`); fields are only added within a schema version, never removed or renamed |
| GitHub Action | input and output names and their meaning; pin a tag or a commit SHA |
| MCP server | tool names, their arguments, and the `status` and `verdict` fields |

Removing or renaming any of these, or changing their meaning, is a breaking change. Adding is not: a new check type, a new report field, or a new `status` value (`inconclusive` was added after 0.2.0). Treat any status you don't know as not passed.

## Deprecation

Before something is removed, it keeps working for at least one minor release with a warning that names the replacement, and the changelog says so. After 1.0, removals wait for the next major version.


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/design-partners/

# Design partners

We want Netdryrun shaped by real changes, not guesses. If you have a routing change coming up, we'll help you test it in a lab, for free, in exchange for honest feedback.

## What you get

- A runnable containerlab lab of the relevant part of your network, built with you from your sanitized configs.
- A `netdryrun.yml` with checks for what your change must do and what must never happen (leaks, lost reachability).
- The verdict with evidence, before your change goes anywhere real. You keep everything.
- Help wiring it into your CI, if you want it there.

## What we ask

- One real upcoming change, and sanitized configs for the routers involved: replace public addresses and AS numbers with documentation ranges and remove secrets. We'll help you check.
- Honest feedback: what was useful, what got in the way, how you test changes today.
- Optional: permission to publish an anonymized write-up. Nothing is published without your written OK.

## Fair warning

- A lab is not production. A pass covers the checks in the lab, on the network OSes we support ([FRR, Nokia SR Linux, SONiC, Arista EOS](reference/config.md#drivers)). See [what a lab cannot prove](trust.md#what-a-lab-cannot-prove).
- We never touch your production network and never need access to it.
- We take a few partners at a time, so each change gets proper attention.

## How your configs are handled

You send sanitized configs only. They're used for your lab and nothing else and kept private. We build labs with the help of Anthropic's Claude, so your configs are processed by it, under terms that don't allow training on them; no other AI service sees them. They're deleted within 30 days after delivery unless you ask us to keep them. An NDA is available on request. See the [privacy notice](privacy.md#configs-you-send-us).

## Apply

Run `netdryrun feedback` and tick "Design partner", or email [hello@netdryrun.com](mailto:hello@netdryrun.com) with one line about the change you want to test.


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/contact/

# Contact

| What | Where | Expect an answer |
|---|---|---|
| Feedback after trying it (2 minutes) | run `netdryrun feedback`, or the [feedback form](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/issues/new?template=feedback.yml) | read by a human |
| Free help testing one real change | [design partners](design-partners.md) | within a few days |
| Bugs, questions, feature requests | [GitHub issues](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/issues) | best effort, usually within a few days |
| Security vulnerabilities (please don't open a public issue) | [security@netdryrun.com](mailto:security@netdryrun.com) or [GitHub private vulnerability reporting](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/security/advisories/new) | acknowledgment within 3 days |
| Everything else: trademark permission, paid work, press | [hello@netdryrun.com](mailto:hello@netdryrun.com) | best effort, usually within a few days |

Netdryrun is a small, independent open-source project. There is no phone line and no sales team. Free use comes with best-effort support; see the [support and versioning policy](support.md).

Security researchers: our [security.txt](https://netdryrun.com/.well-known/security.txt) follows RFC 9116, and the [security policy](https://github.com/netdryrun/netdryrun/blob/main/SECURITY.md) explains how reports are handled.

# Privacy notice

*Last updated: 27 October 2026*

## Who is responsible

Netdryrun is operated by Victor Khen, Taiwan ("we"). Contact for anything about your data: [hello@netdryrun.com](mailto:hello@netdryrun.com).

## The short version

- **The Netdryrun tool** (CLI, GitHub Action, MCP server) has no telemetry. It sends us nothing. The GitHub Action has a `cloud` input reserved for Netdryrun Cloud, a hosted service that is not available yet; setting it today uploads nothing. Its own privacy terms will be published here before it launches.
- **This website** sets no cookies, has no analytics and no forms, and serves its fonts itself.
- **We see your data only if you email us, interact with the project on GitHub, or send us configs as a design partner.**

## This website

netdryrun.com is static documentation hosted on GitHub Pages. To deliver the pages, GitHub processes your IP address and request details (page, time, browser) under the [GitHub privacy statement](https://docs.github.com/en/site-policy/privacy-policies/github-general-privacy-statement). We do not receive these logs. If you switch between light and dark mode, your browser remembers the choice in its local storage; that stays on your device. Search runs entirely in your browser.

## Email

When you write to an @netdryrun.com address, Cloudflare Email Routing forwards the message to our mailbox. We use your address and message only to answer you and keep the conversation for as long as it's useful, then delete it. Security reports may be kept as records of how the issue was handled. Lawful basis: our legitimate interest in answering you.

## Configs you send us

If you are a [design partner](design-partners.md), you send us sanitized configs so we can build a lab of part of your network. We use them only for your lab. We build labs with the help of Anthropic's Claude, so Anthropic processes the configs on our behalf, under commercial terms that don't allow training on them; no other AI service receives them. We delete them within 30 days after delivery unless you ask us to keep them. Lawful basis: your request (the work you asked us to do).

## GitHub and PyPI

Issues, pull requests and discussions on [github.com/netdryrun](https://github.com/netdryrun) are public and governed by GitHub's terms and privacy statement. Downloads from PyPI are handled by the Python Software Foundation under the [PyPI privacy notice](https://policies.python.org/pypi.org/Privacy-Notice/). We don't combine this information with anything else.

## Transfers

GitHub, Cloudflare and Anthropic are based in the United States. Transfers of personal data from the EU or UK rely on the EU-US Data Privacy Framework (and its UK extension) where the company is certified, and on the European Commission's standard contractual clauses otherwise.

## Your rights

You can ask for access to, correction of, or deletion of your personal data, a copy of it, restriction of processing, or object to processing based on legitimate interest. Email [hello@netdryrun.com](mailto:hello@netdryrun.com); we answer within 30 days. You can also complain to your data protection authority.

## Changes

We update this notice when what we do with data changes, for example before Netdryrun Cloud or paid products launch, and change the date at the top.
